en: Preface to the Guide to the Three Sutras of the Buddhas and Patriarchs:
In the Chan school, there is what is known as the "Three Sutras of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. It is unknown from what time this originated, yet it has been transmitted and practiced for a long time.

For the most part, they contain few discourses that are lofty, remote, or vast; rather, they consist entirely of instructions that are immediate and practical for daily life, serving merely to guard against... [text fragment ends]

To admonish frivolous emotions and unwholesome karma, thereby guiding them toward the Right Path, is the primary gateway to studying the Buddha and a precious instruction for enlightening the ignorant.
No one who has become a monk can fail to know this; it is just as when building a mountain nine fathoms high, the work must necessarily begin with a single basket of earth.
If one discards the single basket while discoursing on the nine-fathom peak, even a young child would know that such a thing is impossible.
In recent times, followers of the Chan school have been superficially enamored with the lofty and remote, feeling ashamed to discuss what is humble and near.
Upon seeing such works as these, they invariably shake their heads and disregard them, falsely believing that those of superior faculties and superior wisdom would not deign to engage with this.

They do not realize, however, that those of superior faculties and superior wisdom are precisely those who ought not to exclude the cultivation of the middling and inferior; it was like the Venerable Kāśyapa, who transmitted the robe with a single smile, thereby establishing the Patriarchal School.
The First Patriarch practiced the dhūta austerities with vigor throughout his entire life and never abandoned them; was it that his faculties and wisdom were inferior?
How do the faculties and wisdom of those people today compare to that of Kāśyapa? It is simply that their deluded passions are difficult to restrain and they delight in negligence;
thus, they resort to lofty and distant words to indulge their own private whims. I know that they will surely end up by wallowing in self-indulgence and self-abandonment.
I, Zihui, have here provided my first commentary on this scripture to serve as a guide for beginners;
I have sought to clarify its meaning through inspired exposition, though it may contain but a single basketful of thought.
The Elder Yongjue of Gushan inscribed this at the Shengjian Hall as his own preface:
"The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is lofty and unsurpassed, profound and unfathomable; yet there must be a gate for its realization and a practice for its cultivation."
There must surely be a gradual progression; as for that which may serve as a guide for elementary study and a single step toward the journey of a thousand *li*, is it not the Three Scriptures?
Formerly, when the World-Honored One first attained the Way, the conditions of sentient beings were not yet ripe and they could not yet endure the Great Dharma.

Thus, within the Deer Park, he concealed the ultimate truth and manifested provisional teachings, guiding them skillfully and gradually until the three vehicles and five vehicles were all fully prepared—this was forty years ago.
The second chapter is precisely this. Since all vehicles have already been opened and revealed by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Tathāgata’s work in appearing in the world is thereby completed.

Thus, between the twin trees, he proclaimed his entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; upholding the *vinaya* and discoursing on the eternal, he took these as his final profound instructions—this is the *Śāsanānuśāsana*.
As for these two sutras, although their timing has a beginning and an end, their meaning is in reality not two different tracks; it is simply that the beginning...
Thus, being proximate yet detailed, and ultimately solemn yet urgent, it serves as a high and upright bulwark against the wandering and dissipation of deluded emotions.
Is this not the wondrous skillful means by which the Tathāgata opens up things for beings, and the essential path through which all capacities must pass?

Yet, since the Sage has long been gone and the faculties of sentient beings have daily declined, those who have left the household life often lose the primary cause regarding the Great Master, the Tathāgata.
From beginning to end, his clear instructions were no different from those of a person from Qin looking at the plumpness or emaciation of a person from Yue;

thus, although his shaven head and square-cut robes resembled those of a monk, he was in fact not far removed from the Brahmins—this is why the *Miaoshan Jingce* (The Admonition of Mount Miao) was composed.

Indeed, its words for dispelling chaos and restoring correctness, as well as its warnings to the populace and remedies for societal flaws, deeply capture the bequeathed intent of the Buddhas of the past.
Because these two scriptures have not fallen into oblivion, the ancients combined them and designated them as the "Three Scriptures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs" to transmit to the world.

This ensures that future students, regarding the lofty and profound path of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, will know how to reach their ultimate realization and avoid falling among the unworthy or abandoning their progress halfway;
is the benefit of this not indeed great? (Ru) At the age of twenty, I first performed the ritual of prostration.
When the Old Monk was at Mount He, Master He took pity on my dullness and ignorance and first bestowed upon me these sutras, instructing me to practice them diligently.

It has now been over ten years; that I have entered and emerged from both Chan and doctrinal studies with such tireless devotion, never straying from the Way, is due to the power of these three sutras.
Recently, as there were no affairs in the mountains, a guest questioned me, saying: "In the past, the Great..."
After the ravages of war, Chan Master Hong sui lived on grass and wood, providing commentaries on three sutras for his students;
his words were concise and his principles refined—truly what is called "medicine produced from a golden jar to save the sick.

Now, more than five hundred years have passed since the era of Da-hong, yet the world-path and the Dharma-path afflict one another with ever-increasing intensity. You, my son, are capable [of addressing this].
"Shall I expose my inner store of knowledge to treat you with medicine? I replied, "Indeed; this is my resolve. How could I dare offer any pretexts or decline?
Thus, casting aside my own ignorance and meager learning, I have exerted myself in this task. After one month, the draft was completed, and I inscribed its title as 'The Guide' (*Zhinan*).
This is because I wish that those who have first conceived the intention [to study] may know where to direct their aspirations, so that they do not fall into confusion, error, or missteps."
This has merely entered upon a perilous path; as for whether the medicine accords with the illness or not, I have simply no leisure to deliberate upon it.
This preface to the general principles was written on the first day of the first month of spring in the year of Yiyou.
The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* follows the version annotated by Master Sui; it differs somewhat from the version found in the Tripitaka.
Zhuxiang once examined this matter, asserting that while Master Sui’s text excels both in phrasing and meaning, the Tripitaka version contains many inconsistencies;
therefore, I too now follow Master Sui’s edition.
Regarding the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra*, there was a treatise by Aśvaghoṣa and a commentary by Guishan, both of which have not been transmitted to the world;

what has recently been transmitted is merely the essential extracts from the treatise and commentary by the Song dynasty Master Jingyuan. The Venerable Master Yunqi once provided supplementary annotations for it, and I now rely upon these to compose this exegesis.

The *Cautionary Verses* (Jingce) of Mount Gui Shan appear superficial in their expression yet are profound in their intent; they seem repetitive in their phrasing yet possess a continuous thread of meaning.
Previous commentators, numbering perhaps one or two families, have largely been superficial and failed to grasp the author’s true heart.
Therefore, I have ventured to provide a new commentary.
Master Yunqi Zhuchuang spoke repeatedly on the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* and the *Sūtra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teachings* across several sections;

now, I record one of these to reveal his intent: "Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreamed of a golden man at night and dispatched envoys to India, where they obtained the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.
This was the beginning of the holy teaching flowing eastward into China. Now, by means of this—

Regarding the statement that one should not approach monks who do not maintain their recitations, nor those who do not ascend the seat to lecture for others: these words of the sutra are not exclusively about those who are near;
there are those who are distant, and there are those whose words are near while their meaning is far-reaching, yet people themselves fail to discern this.

Furthermore, the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yijing jing) contains the essential final instructions of the Tathāgata upon his entry into parinirvāṇa, serving as a metaphor for what the world calls a "testament."

For descendants to be oblivious to the origins established by their ancestors is to forget one's roots; for descendants to turn their backs on the final instructions left by their parents at the time of death is to be unfilial.

How can those who have become monks not reflect upon this? I, the humble writer, examine these two scriptures and find them to be truly excellent medicines for curing the ailments of the Dharma-ending age; they must not be neglected, they must not be neglected.

Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty issued an edict on the implementation of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching), in which his exhortations to the monks and nuns were expressed with profound sincerity;
this is appended here to demonstrate the holy sovereign’s intention to protect the Dharma. The Imperial Edict states:

"The Dharma, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, was entrusted to kings and great ministers to uphold and sustain the Buddha-Dharma during this degenerate age of decline. Now, as for the monks and nuns who have left the household life..."

The precepts for the household must be fully observed; if one indulges in lustful excesses, one encounters afflictions at every turn. Such conduct violates the scriptures and the Vinaya in all human dealings;
it not only loses the profound and subtle intent of the Tathāgata but also fails the duty of upholding the King’s entrustment.

The *Śāsanānuśāsanī Sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha on the eve of his parinirvāṇa as an exhortation to his disciples; it is exceedingly detailed and essential for those of the degenerate age, whether monastics or laypeople.
Since the Great Way is not being venerated and profound words are about to vanish into obscurity, I harbor a perpetual longing for the holy teachings and intend to contemplate their wide propagation.

Composed by the Fucha monk Daopei.
*The Sutra of Forty-two Sections Spoken by the Buddha*.
Whenever the Buddha preached a sutra, there was always an introductory context (*nidāna*), whether he ascended the seat to deliver a discourse for a specific person based on a particular event,
or whether he established a title— be it a single name or multiple names— as seen in the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and others. This sutra alone, however,
was taught by the Buddha at the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment, as a spontaneous guidance according to the capacities of beings during his ordinary daily life.

It was not merely for the sake of one person or a single matter; therefore, the teachings he inquired about varied in their scope—whether Great or Small, Sudden or Gradual—and his explanations likewise lacked fixed names.
Later, the compilers of the scriptures organized these into chapters, totaling forty-two;
thus it is titled *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha in Forty-two Chapters*. "The Buddha" refers to the Teacher who is able to speak.
Regarding the titles established for the seven types of dharmas taught in the second chapter, this is a title based on both person and dharma (*pudgala-dharma*).

According to the six types of *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compounds) and *dvandva* (copulative compounds), the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections Spoken by the Buddha* is a *tatpuruṣa* with an accompanying number (*adhikaraṇa-saṃkhyā*).

Furthermore, if the forty-two sections themselves are the sūtra, it is a *karmadhāraya* with an accompanying number. As for "sūtra," it is explained according to the usual interpretation as possessing four characteristics.
"Yi" (義) means to penetrate and encompass the eternal Dharma.
Regarding the Later Han (the Eastern Han), Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna translated [the scriptures] together.
According to the *Liang Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Liang Dynasty), Kāśyapa Mātanga was originally a native of Central India.
He possessed excellent deportment and was proficient in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras; he had long made it his duty to travel for the sake of conversion.
Previously, while traveling through a small tributary state of India, he preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. Upon encountering an invasion by a hostile nation, he thought to himself:
"If one can preach this Dharma, they will be protected by earth deities, causing those who dwell there to enjoy peace and happiness. Now that the clash of weapons has only just begun—"

To benefit [the people], he then made a vow and went in person to mediate and persuade; consequently, the two nations entered into friendly relations, and by this means his reputation became manifest.
During the Yongping era of the Han dynasty, Emperor Ming dreamed of a golden man flying through the air and arriving;
he then assembled his ministers to interpret the dream. The learned official Fu Yi respectfully replied: "Your servant has heard that there is a deity in the Western Regions..."
Their names were [Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna]. "Is it not this that Your Majesty dreamed of? the Emperor thought, and he agreed.
He immediately dispatched Langzhong Cai Yin, the disciple Qin Jing, and others to India to seek out the Buddha-dharma.
While there, Cai Yin and his companions encountered Kāśyapa Mātanga, whom they invited back to China. Mātanga was determined to propagate the teachings and did not shrink from toil or hardship.
Braving the shifting sands of the Flowing Sands, he arrived at Luoyang, where Emperor Ming received him with great honor and provided a vihāra outside the West Gate of the city for him to dwell in;
this was the beginning of the presence of śramaṇas on Han soil.

At that time, as the Great Dharma had only recently been transmitted and there was yet no widespread faith, Kāśyapa Mātanga reserved his profound understanding and translated only the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.
After a short time, he passed away at the residence of Teng in Luoyang; this was the Baima Monastery located outside the Yong Gate to the west of the city of Luoyang.
Zhu Falan was also a native of Central India who recited several tens of thousands of chapters of sutras and treatises, serving as a scholar for the Indian community.
At that time, when Cai Yin had arrived in that country, Zhu Falan and Kāśyapa Mātanga had already entered into an agreement to travel together for the purpose of conversion;
they subsequently accompanied him on his journey. Upon meeting the local disciples, who were obstructing their progress, Falan traveled by a secret route and arrived at Luoyang.

There he stayed with Kāśyapa Mātanga for a short while and soon became proficient in the Chinese language. As for the scriptures Cai Yin had obtained in the Western Regions, he immediately [began to]...

The translations include five works: the *Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika*), the *Severing of Bonds* (*Saṃyojanasamuccheda*), the *Buddha’s Previous Births* (*Jātaka*), the *Dharma Ocean Treasury* (*Dharmasāgara-kośa*), and the *Buddha’s Original Deeds* (*Buddhacarita*).
Later, due to the turmoil of banditry and the relocation of the capital, four of these works lost their original manuscripts and were no longer transmitted;
only the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* remains extant today, consisting of approximately two thousand words. Among all the scriptures currently preserved in the land of Han, this alone survives.

Shuo replied that he did not know and suggested one might ask the Hu people from the Western Regions. Later, after Dharmaratna arrived, the multitude questioned him about it.
Dharmaratna said, "When the world comes to an end, the kalpa-fire burns through everything; these ashes are the remains of that. Thus, the words of Dongfang Shuo were proven to be true and credible.

After the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, he reflected thus: "Detachment from desire and the stilling of strife are the most supreme states; one should dwell in great meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)."

Having definitively subdued the various māras and paths, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths in the Deer Park, delivering the five men beginning with Kauṇḍinya so that they realized the fruits of the Path.
Furthermore, when bhikṣus had various doubts regarding what was said, they sought the Buddha’s guidance;
the World-Honored One instructed them, awakening each one to understanding. They joined their palms in respectful assent and followed his commands.

"Attaining the Way" refers to attaining the Unsurpassed Way beneath the Bodhi tree. "Contemplating after attaining the Way" refers to his contemplation while gazing at the tree for twenty-one days following his enlightenment.
"Freedom from desire and tranquility" refers to the methods of provisional skillful means he contemplated for the purpose of manifesting transformation:
freedom from desire serves to eliminate afflictions and delusions, while tranquility serves to realize the fruit of cessation (*nirvāṇa*). These two are the essentials for escaping suffering.

Because it serves as the introductory prelude for the Three Vehicles, it is called the "Supreme Abode. Regarding the subduing of Māra: when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, Māra came to disturb him;
therefore, he did not rise from his *nāga*-like state (the meditative posture) but instead subdued him. The Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*) was an ancient imperial park where deer were raised.
The Four Truths—suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—are the two sets of causes, namely those pertaining to the mundane and the supramundane.
When the five men heard that the Prince had entered the mountains and the Father King was grieving for him,
they commanded three of their kinsmen— namely Ābhivarta and Kauṣṭhila— and two of their maternal uncles— namely Kauṇḍinya and Daśabala-Kāśyapa— to go in search of him to serve as his attendants.
They practiced asceticism together with him, consuming only one grain of hemp and one grain of rice per day, or eating such a meal only once every seven days.
For six full years, his body had become emaciated like withered wood. The Bodhisattva thought to himself, "To extinguish heterodox views, I have practiced self-starvation, which is not the Way.
I must accept food before I can attain Buddhahood. He immediately rose from his seat and went to a river to bathe.
There, a cowherd girl—actually a goddess from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven—urged him to offer her milk-gruel. He then accepted it and presented it to her.

As he recited the incantations and offered blessings while receiving food, the five men were startled and thought he had regressed from his practice; they each returned to their respective dwellings and continued to cultivate different methods.
Once the Buddha had attained the Way, he reflected that the conditions for these five men were now ripe and that he could preach the Dharma for them.
Thereupon, he went to the Deer Park and turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times. Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first to attain awakening, and the other four did as well.

Awakening one after another, they were addressed by the Buddha with "Come, O Bhikṣu," whereupon their hair and beards fell away naturally and they all became śramaṇas, realizing the state of Arhatship.

"Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "mendicant" (qǐshì), also as "one who destroys evil" (pò'è), and also as "one who terrifies Māra" (bùmó). These correspond to the three meanings of the fruit of Arhatship:

being worthy of offerings (yīnggòng), slayer of thieves (sházéi), and non-arising (wúshēng). The World-Honored One’s attainment of enlightenment is the Buddha-Jewel. [The teaching of] the Four Noble Truths...
The Dharma is the Jewel, and the Sangha of the five bhikṣus is the Jewel; from this point on, the Three Jewels have remained in the world as the foremost field of merit for humans and devas.
Furthermore, there were those who followed the five [bhikṣus] as monks, such as the three Kāśyapas, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana.
All of them had long served non-Buddhist paths and attained nothing at all; having now encountered the Buddha, it was like [a man with] eyesight entering the light after being in darkness.
Obtaining the lamp is like a poor person finding treasure; therefore, it is said that one seeks the Buddha’s guidance regarding the doubts within one's own mind.
The World-Honored One’s instructions awaken one to each point, as exemplified by the following forty-two chapters.

Furthermore, while other sutras all possess the three divisions of introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*dharmadeśanā*), and the dissemination (*parīndanā*), this sutra alone condenses these three parts within its introduction into a single unit.

This chapter is a distinct example that differs from the common format. From the moment the World-Honored One attained enlightenment until he realized the fruit of the Way, this constitutes the Introductory Section (*nidāna*).
Furthermore, the arrival of the bhikṣus and their successive awakenings constitute the Main Section (*samyak-siddhānta*).

Their joining of palms in respectful assent and compliance with the Honored One’s instructions constitute the Dissemination Section (*pariṇāmanā*). The following forty-two chapters are listed separately.
This is the orthodox tradition; however, as this section is an introduction provided by the compiler of the sutra rather than the Buddha’s own direct teaching, it is treated as a separate chapter.
The Buddha said: "One who leaves home out of a close kinship with the Dharma, recognizes the mind and penetrates its source, and understands the unconditioned dharma is called a śramaṇa.
Constantly practicing the two hundred and fifty precepts, pure in every movement and stillness, one cultivates the four true paths of practice and becomes an arhat. Arhat...
The Han [spirit] is able to fly and undergo transformations, possesses a lifespan spanning vast kalpas, and can cause heaven and earth to shake;
next is the Anāgāmin. The Anāgāmin, at the end of his life, ascends as a spiritual consciousness to the nineteenth heaven to realize Arhatship.
Next is the Sakṛdāgāmin. The Sakṛdāgāmin goes up once and returns once more before attaining Arhatship. Next is the Srotāpanna. The Srotāpanna...

The *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) undergoes seven deaths and seven births before realizing *arhatship*. One whose craving for desire is severed is like one whose four limbs have been amputated and can no longer be used;
this demonstrates the dharma of the śramaṇa.
"Śramaṇa" is a Sanskrit term translated here as "diligent cessation," meaning to diligently cultivate the three trainings.
The extinction of the three poisons is the essence of the śramaṇa’s departure from home and family. To realize that objects are but consciousness is called "knowing the mind";
to know the Dharma is to realize its nature, which is called "awakening to the root. Since the self-nature of the five aggregates is originally unarisen, it is now without cessation;
