The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teachings.
The Dharma-realm True Body is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; out of compassionate vows for the sake of sentient beings, it manifests coming and going.
As for what is called the *Buddha-śāsana-sūtra*, every Buddha, at the time of his passing into extinction, preaches this sūtra. This is the *Śāsana-sūtra* of our Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
"Śāsana" (遗教) refers to the remaining dharma-words left behind to instruct and admonish all capacities of beings. The fourfold assembly of disciples...
My son, in this sutra, the instructions addressed solely to the bhikṣus demonstrate the characteristics of detachment.
Although there are both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna bhikṣus, the fact that only the Hīnayāna methods are shown here is because the expedient means for entering the Path are the same.

However, one must not see only what is shown as being small and consequently claim that this sutra belongs to the Tripiṭaka-teaching (Zàngjiào). This is because it upholds the Vinaya while discussing the Eternal (Cháng).
This distinguishes it from the teachings of the *Pitaka*.
It is also titled *The Sūtra of Brief Instructions Spoken by the Buddha on the Verge of Nirvāṇa*.
"Verge" (*chui*) means to approach; "verge of nirvāṇa" is equivalent to saying "at the time of death. *Nirvāṇa* is translated here as "extinction and deliverance" (*mie-du*).
Regarding *parinirvāṇa*, according to the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) school, there are four kinds of nirvana: first, nirvana of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*);

second, nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); third, nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*); and fourth, non-abiding nirvana (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*). What is now called "approaching nirvana" refers to nirvana without remainder;
yet in reality, it does not depart from the nirvana of intrinsic purity. This is a brief explanation of the instructions.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* has already explained this extensively; however, as the time for his parinirvāṇa arrived at midnight on the fifteenth day of the second month,
he further instructed the assembly present before him and the disciples of future generations with words of urgent importance,
and thus it is said that he spoke briefly.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin [Dynasty].
"Yaoqin" refers to Yao Xing of the Later Qin, who succeeded the Eastern Jin.

A "Tripiṭaka Master" (Sanzang Fashi) is one who has mastered the three collections of the Dharma—the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—and serves as a teacher for ten thousand generations. "Kumārajīva" is translated here as "Child Longevity" (Tongshou). This means:
Though he was young in years, he possessed the virtues of the aged. The translation of this meaning is as explained above.

When the Master was invited by the Lord of Qin to enter China, he translated sutras and śāstras to propagate the Buddha Vehicle; his great achievements and eminent virtues are fully recorded in his biography.
According to the Great Outline of the Treatise by the Patriarch Aśvaghoṣa, it is divided into seven sections:

First, the Introduction (while most sūtras clarify three divisions—namely the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination—the Introduction further distinguishes between the "Certification of Faith" and the "Initiation";
in this present sūtra, the Certification of Faith is missing from the Introduction and the Dissemination is entirely absent; this pattern is identical to that of the *Heart Sūtra*).
When Śākyamuni Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, he delivered the Arhats Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others;
finally, when preaching the Dharma, he delivered Subhadra. Those who were to be saved have all been saved.
Between the twin śāla trees, as he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, it was the middle of the night, silent and still; for his disciples, he briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma.
Śākya is translated here as "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren); it is his clan name. Muni is translated as "Silent Sage" (Jimo).
Kauṇḍinya was seen previously; Subhadra is translated as "Virtuous and Wise. He was a non-Buddhist who resided in the city of Kuśinagara.

At the age of one hundred and twenty, hearing that the Buddha had entered *parinirvāṇa*, he finally went to the Buddha’s location. The Buddha extensively expounded the Four Noble Truths for him, and he attained realization.
"Arhat" means "Sāla," which is translated here as "firm and solid. Regarding the "pair of trees": the upper branches meet and the lower roots are joined;
one withers while the other flourishes, symbolizing the destruction of the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. The "middle night" symbolizes the Middle Way.
"Silence" symbolizes that the self-nature is free from discursive thought, and "the absence of sound" symbolizes that the self-nature is beyond words. This is the introduction to this sutra.
The various sūtras differ because while other sūtras provide an introduction only for that specific scripture, this sūtra provides a general introduction to the entire dispensation;

therefore, it cannot be constrained by ordinary conventions. The initial teaching that delivered Kātyāyana marks the beginning of the introduction, and the final delivery of Subhadra marks the end of the introduction.
Between the twin trees, as he was about to enter nirvāṇa, the introduction to the manifestation [of the teaching] concludes.
That it was at this time, during the silence of midnight, demonstrates the preliminary sign of his entry into *nirvāṇa*.
That he briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for his disciples means that while he had previously explained them extensively, he now merely cites their essential points.
Thus one knows that this sutra is the final expression of the Tathāgata’s profound compassion; though the text is not voluminous, every word is vital and essential.
Those who have truly left the household life should pay close attention to this.
II. The Section on Cultivating Worldly Merits (The teachings presented in this section consist of methods for destroying the three obstructions and escaping the four miserable destinies;
as they do not yet discuss escaping the three realms, they are referred to simply as "worldly merits. This section is divided into seven parts.)
First, regarding the cessation of wrong actions (this section refers to the four kinds of wrong actions that are to be restrained):
"O Bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should revere, treasure, and respect the Prātimokṣa as those who encounter light in the darkness or as a poor man who finds a treasure;
know that this is your true Teacher. Even if I were to remain in the world,"
Apart from these, those who uphold the pure precepts must not engage in buying or selling, nor establish fields and houses, nor keep people, slaves, or livestock;
they must avoid all cultivation of plants and all accumulation of wealth and treasures as if avoiding a pit of fire.
They must not cut down grass or trees, nor dig the earth or excavate the soil, nor compound medicinal decoctions, nor practice divination for good or ill fortune. They must look upward...

Observing the stars, calculating the movements of the waxing and waning of the calendar, and performing astrological computations—none of these should be practiced. One must restrain the body, eat at the proper times, and maintain a pure livelihood.
One must not involve oneself in worldly affairs, nor employ life-prolonging incantations, worldly spells, or elixirs of immortality.

One must not cultivate intimacy with the noble or engage in familiar, disrespectful behavior; all such things are improper. One should instead rectify one's own mind, maintain right mindfulness, and seek liberation, never harboring deceit.

One should conceal flaws and manifest excellence to avoid deluding the masses; regarding the four types of offerings, one should know moderation and contentment, accepting whatever requisites are obtained without hoarding them.

This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of upholding the precepts (*śīla*). Since the precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation, they are called *prātimokṣa*.
By relying on these precepts, one attains the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should maintain pure precepts and not allow them to be broken or deficient.
If a person can maintain pure precepts, they will be able to possess wholesome dharmas; if there are no pure precepts, all various wholesome merits cannot arise.
For this reason, you should know that the precepts are the foremost dwelling place for the merit of peace and security.

The text is divided into four sections: first, the honoring of the precepts; second, the upholding of the precepts; third, the praising of the precepts; and fourth, the concluding exhortation. This is the first section.
The address "You, bhikṣus" is like a worldly parent on the verge of death calling out to their children and grandchildren to give them final instructions;

the World-Honored One acts likewise here, which represents his ultimate and profound compassion. The following sections should be understood in this same manner. This concludes the first two [sections].
The first line correctly exhorts one to honor the *prātimokṣa*, which refers to the monastic precepts;

this is called "individual liberation" (*pratimokṣa*), meaning that by upholding each individual precept, one attains a corresponding liberation. The following two lines clarify the power and function of the precepts:

just as one who encounters light when in darkness crosses over the obstacle of afflictions, or as a poor person obtains treasure, they cross over the obstacle of lacking roots of goodness; such is their power.
"By means of this, one may indeed show respect"—the latter three phrases demonstrate that the precepts are the Buddha.

This means that when the Tathāgata dwells in the world, he constantly instructs people using the *pien-zu* (the categories of training rules). As long as these dharmas exist, it is as if the Buddha has not entered parinirvāṇa, because the precepts constitute the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, one must show respect. "Second, maintaining pure precepts" and below clarify the practice of upholding the precepts.

The phrase "Pure Precepts" (*śīla*) serves as a general heading; it cannot be followed by a detailed explanation of the characteristics of maintaining the precepts, which consists of four sections, all of which embody both prohibitive and exhortative meanings.
Generally, the two characters "not to obtain" (*bùdé*) function as a prohibition.

Once the prohibition has been established, there follows the sense of exhortation, as seen in words such as "all should," "and should," and "should oneself," which correspond to one another throughout. Although...
Those who possess both [wealth and status] likewise possess the same intent in their initial stage:
those who engage in buying, selling, and trade follow the path of merchants seeking profit through expedient means; those who establish fields and houses harbor the worldly mind that seeks security;
those who raise subjects increase their external retinue, thereby merely fostering deluded attachment; and those who keep slaves...
Cultivating pride and luxury makes it difficult to give rise to a humble mind; raising livestock is a cause for seeking profit through exploitation and theft;
all forms of planting are occupations that benefit agricultural fields;
and as for various treasures and wealth, because wealth can harm integrity and foster greed, a bhikṣu should remain pure and non-active.
How could one practicing the Dharma of renunciation emulate the ways of the laity to increase their transgressions?
Therefore, one should avoid them as if they were a pit of fire. In the subsequent section, cutting down trees and grass destroys the villages of spirits and violates compassion;
tilling the soil and digging the earth harms living beings and constitutes wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Compounding medicinal decoctions... [and so forth].
This means that the study of medicine, physiognomy, astronomy, calendrical calculations, and the like are all occupations for sustaining one's life through wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
A *bhikṣu*, whose resolve is set upon seeking liberation, ought to restrain his body, eat at the proper times, and maintain a pure livelihood;
how could he, for the sake of seeking gain and offerings, harm living beings, injure life, and allow his mind to run toward various arts? One must exercise restraint.
"Body" refers to regulating the body so that it does not become dissipated or over-exerted. "Eating at the proper time" means not eating after midday.
"Pure livelihood" means either begging for food or receiving offerings from donors; this is called right livelihood, while all other forms are wrong livelihood.
"Three types of worldly affairs" refer to matters concerning kings, officials, and even matters involving relatives and laypeople.
"Acting as a messenger" refers to serving as a courier for the noble and powerful, conveying letters back and forth.

"Sorcery" refers to relying on heterodox incantations to harass and disturb sentient beings. "Elixirs of the immortals" refers to relying on heterodox medicinal potions while falsely hoping to prolong one's lifespan.

"Cultivating intimacy" refers to such things as baring one's shoulders with sycophancy, laughing with flattery, and adopting the cringing, servile demeanor of a slave. "Noble persons" refers to those of distinguished lineage, power, and influence who are treated with familiarity.
This refers to becoming intimately familiar with such things. Now, a bhikṣu is one who stands beyond the world; he does not serve kings or lords, for he holds his practice in high esteem.
How could he allow himself to enter the realm of the mundane, let his mind be defiled by heterodox arts, and thus bring himself to degradation?
Therefore, it is right that he should rectify his mind and maintain right mindfulness in order to seek liberation. These four sections conceal flaws and blemishes.
"Concealing one's own faults" means hiding one's transgressions. "Displaying wonders to delude the masses" means causing others to have incorrect understanding.
The Royal Code states: "One who causes confusion among the multitude shall be executed. The Vinaya says: "One who claims to have attained the state of an Arhat commits a *pārājika* offense.

These are all cases where, due to an internal loss of right mindfulness, one externally startles others with heterodox paths; neither is something a bhikṣu should do. The "four types of offerings" refer to the four requisites, namely: [food, clothing, bedding, and medicine].
To know the proper measure regarding clothing, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, and bedding means not to take more than necessary;
to be content means not to crave what is fine. Regarding that which should not be stored: formerly there was a bhikṣu who begged extensively and accumulated wealth;

neither practicing the Path nor performing meritorious deeds, he later received the retribution of being reborn as a large fish. Today’s bhikṣus likewise do not practice the Path, yet they accumulate provisions.
Wealth is a debt incurred for future lives that must be repaid; since it can never be fully settled, is this not a great suffering?

Therefore, it is something one ought not to pursue. This concludes the brief explanation of the characteristics of upholding the precepts. The phrase "The three precepts are correct" serves as the summary of upholding the precepts.
The following section clarifies the praise of the precepts, specifically to distinguish the correct from the deviant and to accord with liberation through understanding.
"Fundamental" refers to *nirvāṇa* and the Noble Path, which are established by means of this. Regarding "relying on this precept and so forth," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"From the precept arises concentration; from concentration, wisdom is developed. This implies that the precept can give rise to concentration and the precept can give rise to wisdom—this is the ultimate praise of the precept.
"Therefore, bhikṣus... and below concludes with an exhortation: one who is able to uphold the precepts [will attain these benefits].
Thus, those who possess wholesome dharmas are able to generate concentration and wisdom through the precepts, whereas those without the precepts are the opposite.
For this reason, although there are many places of security and peace, the precepts are foremost among them. Question:

Regarding what has been refuted above, why is it that all instances involve the light precepts while the heavy precepts are not mentioned? Answer: Even the light precepts are still subject to prohibition; how much more so the heavy ones?
This can be understood. Nevertheless, how can one know that what is being prohibited is not merely a lure for lust, killing, theft, and falsehood?
To forestall evil in its incipiency and prevent it before it manifests is the intention of the Buddha; is this not something we ought to examine?
Second, the admonition to restrain the senses and the mind:
"O bhikṣus, since you are already able to abide in the precepts, you should now restrain the five sense faculties so that they do not become heedless and enter into the five desires.
It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over his herd, not allowing them to run wild and trample the crops. If he were to let them loose..."
The five faculties are not merely the five desires; they are boundless and cannot be restrained.
They are like unruly horses that, if not controlled by a bridle, will drag a person down into a pit (the same as *kan*).

While the suffering of being robbed or harmed lasts but a single lifetime, the calamity of the thieves of the five faculties extends through successive generations; their harm is extremely grave and one must not fail to be cautious. Therefore, the wise person—
Restrain them and do not follow after them; maintain them as if they were thieves, not allowing them to run wild.
Even if you were to let them loose, they would all soon be seen to perish. These five faculties have the mind as their master; therefore, you should skillfully restrain the mind.
The dreadfulness of the mind exceeds that of venomous snakes, evil beasts, hostile robbers, or great fires; even the latter are insufficient to serve as metaphors for it.
It is like a person holding a vessel of honey who, moving about restlessly, looks only at the honey and fails to see the deep pit;
or like a mad elephant without a goad, or a monkey that has found a tree and leaps and bounds about, difficult to restrain—one must swiftly subdue it lest it become unrestrained.
To let this mind run wild destroys one's wholesome deeds; to control it in a single place leads to no trouble.
Because these [senses] are not yet mastered, a bhikṣu should apply himself with diligent vigor to subdue his own mind.
Having been able to abide in the first phrase regarding the precepts, one should next restrain the lower precepts; this first clarifies the method for restraining the sense-faculties.

The text is divided into three sections: first, the Dharma; second, the analogy; and third, the concluding exhortation. This is the first section. The five faculties refer to the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body.

Because the tongue and the body each give rise to consciousness, they receive the designation of "roots" (*indriya*). The five desires (*pañca-kāma*) refer to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
alternatively, it is said they are wealth, form, fame, food, and sleep, so called because they can give rise to the mind's need and longing.
To "restrain" means to subdue and tame them. Master Sui said: "The preceding was establishing precepts based on specific events to prevent wrongdoing and stop evil; now..."
To clearly and carefully guard the gates of the sense-faculties, one must constantly exercise restraint. There are three analogies below; first, the analogy of the cowherd.
The "cow" represents the five sense-faculties, the "person" represents the bhikṣu, the "staff" represents the observance of the precepts, and the "crops" represent the objects of the five desires.
This means that if the cow is not tended, it will damage the crops; likewise, if the faculties are not restrained, they will enter into the five desires. If...

Although the five faculties are not limited to the five objects of desire, it is because the habitual tendencies of the faculties and desires of sentient beings have soaked in and become as firmly fixed as oil mixed into flour;
if they are not urgently restrained, the waves of consciousness will surge forth boundlessly and cannot be stopped.
Second, the analogy of the two evil horses: "horses" also refers to the faculties; "not restraining with a bridle" means not [restraining them].

This is because they are restrained by the precepts. The metaphor of falling into a pit or a ditch illustrates sinking into the evil realms; the destruction of crops represents the cause, while falling into the pit or ditch represents the result.
The three types of thieves illustrate how the light case serves as a comparison for the heavy one:

whereas ordinary thieves harm the physical body and thus their suffering lasts but a single lifetime, those who damage the faculties destroy the life-force of wisdom, and thus their calamities extend through successive kalpas. Therefore, the wise [should]—as concluded below—exhort others to exercise restraint.
Yet one does not follow after the fetters of cattle or horses, holding them as if they were bandits who plunder and harm; even if one were to release them, they would soon perish.
This refers to the pleasures of the five desires, which are like sparks from a stone or a flash of lightning that vanish instantly and are not worth indulging in.
These five faculties have the mind as their master. Next follows the section clarifying the restraint of the mind, which is divided into four parts. First:

This section consists of four parts: (1) the Dharma, (2) the three metaphors, (3) the comparison of gains and losses, and (4) the concluding exhortation. This is the first part. Regarding "the mind": this refers to the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Because it alone is the primary factor that moves the body and initiates speech, it is designated as the "master.

In the phrase "the dreadfulness of the two minds," the following four metaphors—such as the venomous snake and so forth—illustrate the three poisons along with their equal proportions (*sāmya*). That is to say, this mind may suddenly become angry, which is like poison.
The serpent’s desire to sting a person arises suddenly through delusion (*moha*); the wild beast’s desire to pounce on a person arises suddenly through greed (*lobha*);
and the enemy bandit’s desire to plunder a person arises through the equal combination (*samabhāga*) of these factors.

These are like a great fire that leaps forth and consumes both jade and stone alike. These three analogies—the serpent, the beast, and the bandit—illustrate ignorance (*ajñāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), specifically referring to ignorance.
A mind that thinks only of the five desires and disregards the three miserable realms is like seeing honey without seeing the pit.
Furthermore, a restless mind is light, frivolous, and agitated, like an unhooked elephant or a monkey that has found a tree; it is difficult to control.
What is meant by "swiftly suppressing" is that as soon as a subtle thought stirs, one must sever it with fierce force; there should be no delay.
"Relaxing" refers to relaxing this mind to examine its progress and shortcomings; this "mind" is what is called the *manovijñāna* (consciousness).

When one relaxes the mind, the spirit runs toward objects of desire and the faculties become wild and dissolute; consequently, neither worldly nor world-transcending virtues can be accomplished, which is why it is said that one "loses the good deeds of a person.
One who restrains the mind turns the light inward, gathers their thoughts, and applies their will without division; thus, whatever they aspire to must necessarily be achieved.
Because it has been attained, it is said that "there is no task it cannot accomplish. For this reason, the conclusion below offers an exhortation: this mind is like a venomous snake;
since it is so fearsome and difficult to restrain, who but one who exerts diligent effort (*vīrya*) could subdue it?
Yongjia said: "The depletion of the wealth of Dharma and the destruction of merit—none arise except from this mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*). Therefore, in the Chan gate...

"Having thoroughly understood the mind, one suddenly enters non-arising; by the power of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), it is solely through this power of knowledge and vision that one can understand the mind and enter non-arising.

Furthermore, Linji said: "If one can, in a single thought-moment, realize that conditioned arising is non-arising and transcend the views of those who study the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles—if one can truly do so, this is genuine diligence."
The Third Admonition on Avoiding Excessive Seeking:
"You bhikṣus, when receiving various foods and drinks, you should regard them as taking medicine. Whether they are good or bad, do not give rise to feelings of preference or aversion.
Seek only to sustain the body and eliminate hunger and thirst, just as a bee gathering from flowers takes only its nectar without damaging its color or fragrance."
The bhikṣu is likewise: receiving the offerings of others, he proceeds to eliminate his own afflictions and does not seek much, lest he ruin his wholesome mind.
It is like a wise man who calculates the amount of strength a cow can bear and does not exceed its limit so as to exhaust its power.
There are three parables in total to admonish against excessive seeking. First, the parable of taking medicine: "increasing or decreasing" is equivalent to "accepting or rejecting.

This means that food is used to satisfy hunger just as medicine is used to cure disease; why then should one practice both acceptance and rejection? Second, the parable of the two bees and the flower:

this refers to not damaging the color or fragrance, meaning one must not seek excessively so as to destroy the virtuous mind of the donor. Finally, "seeking only to remove one's own afflictions" means...
A bhikṣu accepts offerings merely to remove the affliction of hunger and thirst; what need is there for excessive seeking? The analogy of the three oxen illustrates this:
one must weigh the strength of the oxen, which means reflecting upon one’s own virtuous conduct. If the burden placed upon the oxen exceeds their capacity, they will exhaust their strength;
likewise, if a bhikṣu accepts alms in excess of his needs, he will ruin his path.
The Fourth Admonition on Sleep:
"You bhikṣus, by day you should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and not let the time pass in vain; during the first and last watches of the night, do not neglect your practice either;
in the middle watch, recite the sūtras to refresh yourselves. Do not, for the sake of sleep, allow even a single..."
To give rise to [the thought of] emptiness is a fault, for there is nothing to be attained. You should contemplate that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds;
seek early deliverance for yourself and do not sleep! The thieves of affliction constantly watch for the opportunity to kill you, even more so than an enemy;
how can you sleep without awakening yourself? The venomous snake of affliction sleeps within your heart, like a black viper in your room.
One should use the hook of moral discipline to expel drowsiness early; only when the serpent of sleep has been driven out can one sleep in peace.
To sleep while it has not been expelled is the mark of a person devoid of shame. Among all forms of adornment, the garment of shame is supreme.
Shame is like an iron hook that can restrain a person from what is unrighteous. Therefore, a bhikṣu should always maintain a sense of shame and never allow it to lapse for even a moment.

If one is devoid of shame and modesty, then all virtues will be lost; a person who possesses a sense of shame possesses wholesome dharmas, whereas one who lacks shame is no different from birds and beasts.
The text is divided into three sections: first, the formal admonition against sleep; second, the instruction to apply the antidote of observation;

and third, the instruction to give rise to shame and remorse. This is the first section. There are three types of sleep: first, that arising from food; second, that arising from the passage of time; and third, that arising from the mind.
The first two types are the sleep of an Arhat, because for him there is no mental sleep and the hindrance of torpor has been exhausted. During the day...
One should diligently prepare food and rise from sleep at night without neglecting one's duties; when it is time to rise, one must not let sleep pass in vain.
In summary, both of these matters are governed by the diligent application of *vīrya* (exertion). By means of sleep, the mind becomes clouded and the body grows weary and indolent.
Long ago, the Buddha rebuked Aniruddha, saying: "Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like a snail or a clam!"
First, because one might sleep for a thousand years without hearing the name of the Buddha, it is essential to dispel [this drowsiness].

Second, one should contemplate impermanence (*anitya*) as the antidote through lower-level observation; this primarily treats mental drowsiness, while the other two types of drowsiness are treated concurrently.

First, observe impermanence. There are two kinds of impermanence: the coarse and the subtle. The arising and ceasing of a single lifetime is the coarse; the arising and ceasing of every moment is the subtle.
"Subtle" refers to the world of sentient beings and the physical environment being swallowed by impermanence, like fire consuming wood, perishing moment by moment;

how can one look upon this and sleep peacefully? Next, contemplate the afflictions: the three poisons of affliction lie dormant within the mind, constantly watching for an opportunity to slay the life-force of wisdom.
One should regard these as more formidable than an enemy, for while an enemy kills only the body, [afflictions kill] the life-force.
If one harbors the harmful mind of the three poisons for a single lifetime, its calamity will extend through successive kalpas; how then can one sleep in peace?

Furthermore, the meaning of the "slumbering mind" of affliction is difficult to perceive, whereas the matter of a black viper sleeping in its den is easy to understand; therefore, this is raised again as a metaphor.
Later, one is made to uphold the precepts; the hook of the precepts serves to expel and eliminate [afflictions], for using the precepts to remove delusion is like using a hook to extract a snake.

This statement regarding the precepts concomitant with concentration means that, taken collectively, they use morality to guard against external influences and concentration to clarify the internal mind;

thus, one is able to give rise to wisdom and sever delusions. The phrase "once the sleeping snake has been expelled, one may sleep in peace" means that when the three poisons have been eliminated and one has emerged from the three realms, one can find rest within the abode of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
If, however, the afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been subdued and one indulges in unrestrained conduct...

To sleep peacefully while empty-handedly wasting one’s days—how could this not be the act of a person devoid of shame? The three types of shame constitute a garment that brings about a sense of remorse.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Shame (*hrī*) is internal self-reproach; remorse (*apatrāpya*) is confessing one's faults to others.
Among all forms of adornment, these are the foremost, for it is through precept, concentration, and wisdom that the Dharma-body is adorned.
Only through a sense of shame and dread of blame can one truly practice and learn; therefore, it stands foremost. Why is this?
Because shame can restrain what is improper, just as a hook can subdue an elephant. For this reason, monks, you must not for even a moment be parted from shame and dread of blame.
Possessing shame and dread of blame, one is able to cultivate wholesome dharmas; lacking shame and dread of blame, one has no regard or restraint, and all manner of evils become possible.
If one acts thus, there is little difference between oneself and the beasts.
Regarding the fifth precept against anger:
"O bhikṣus, if someone should come and cut you limb from limb, you should restrain your own mind and not give way to hatred."
One should likewise guard one’s speech and refrain from uttering evil words; for if one gives rein to a mind of anger, it obstructs one’s own path and causes the loss of merit.
The virtue of patience is such that it cannot be equaled by the observance of precepts or ascetic practices. Only one who can practice patience may be called a powerful person of great stature.
If one cannot joyfully endure the poison of foul abuse as if drinking ambrosia, [one is not yet a true practitioner].
Such a person is not called one who has entered the path of wisdom. Why is this? The harm of anger destroys all wholesome dharmas and ruins a good reputation;
it causes people to dislike seeing one in both this life and future lives. You should know that an angry mind is more fierce than a raging fire;
you must always guard against it so that it does not enter. No thief of merit surpasses anger, even among laypeople.
To indulge in sensual desires while not being one who practices the Way, and to lack self-restraint such that one harbors anger, may still be excused.

However, for one who has left the household life to practice the Way—a person free from desire—to harbor hatred and resentment is utterly unacceptable. It is like a thunderclap striking fire within clear, cool clouds;
it is simply not what ought to be.
The text is divided into four sections: first, instructing one to guard the three karmas; second, praising the superior power of patience; third, exposing the grave afflictions of anger;

and fourth, comparing and demonstrating its inappropriateness. This is the first section. If one does not harbor anger when being dismembered, one guards the two karmas of body and mind; if one refrains from uttering evil words, one guards the karma of speech.
If one can refrain from anger even when the body is being killed, the rest may be inferred. For even if one indulges in resentment, it will only obstruct the Path.

One who loses the benefits of merit does so because the fire of anger burns the mind, obstructing one’s own path of practice and causing harm through harsh speech toward others, thereby losing the benefit of transforming others;
thus, it must not be indulged. Regarding the virtue of the two types of patience (*kṣānti*), the following praises the superior power of patience.

There are three kinds: first, patience in enduring enmity and injury; second, patience in calmly accepting suffering; and third, patience in the discernment of dharmas. [This concludes the section on] maintaining ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Those who fall short in asceticism are surpassed by those high in precepts; those who disdain the world and torment themselves are often full of anger toward others, whereas those who practice patience regard enemies and kin with equality, seeing both suffering and joy as equally tranquil.
Furthermore, while precepts and generosity lead to rebirth in the heavens, patience leads one into the Path—how can the former ever compare?
One who is able to endure is called a "powerful great man," for they cannot be disturbed by adverse winds; thus it is said.
Because one who possesses power commits offenses without seeking retribution, they are called "Great Entry," which is like drinking nectar—meaning one experiences it with joy.
Yongjia said: "Let others slander me; let others be wrong. Holding a torch to burn the heavens is merely to exhaust oneself.
When I hear them, it is as if drinking nectar; it melts away and suddenly enters the inconceivable. This is precisely what is meant. As for the passage beginning "Why is this so?"... [end of excerpt]
The "emergence of the grave affliction of anger" refers to the sprouting of evil thoughts that destroy all wholesome dharmas. "Ruining a good reputation" refers to the spreading of an ill repute.

"That which people do not wish to see" refers to the physical manifestation of a wrathful countenance. The "fierce fire and bandits" serve as a general metaphor for the destruction of wholesome dharmas;
as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of hindrance open."
Furthermore, it is clearly inappropriate for laypeople to be compared with monastics; laypeople indulge in sensual desires while bhikṣus practice the Path.
Laypeople lack the Dharma for self-governance, whereas bhikṣus possess the Dharma for self-governance. How can these two be discussed as equals?
Thus, while the anger of a layperson may still be excusable, a bhikṣu harboring anger is utterly unacceptable. It is like a thunderbolt striking amidst clear, cool clouds.
The analogy of the layers of fire illustrates the meaning of what is unacceptable.
The sixth admonition against arrogance states:
"O bhikṣus, you should rub your own heads to cast off ornaments and fine clothing, don robes of dyed color, and carry the alms-bowl."
One begs for one's own livelihood and perceives it thus: "If arrogance should arise, I must quickly extinguish it.
For even increasing arrogance is not appropriate for a layperson in the secular world, let alone for one who has left home to enter the Path.
Is it not for the sake of liberation that one humbles oneself and practices begging?
"Touching one's own head" means fearing that one might forget the mind of renunciation, thereby causing oneself to be awakened and alert.

This first phrase serves as the general summary. The four phrases concerning "discarding fine clothing, wearing coarse garments, holding the alms-bowl, and begging for food" serve as the specific details.

The final phrase, "seeing it thus for oneself," briefly concludes the preceding meaning, signifying: "I have already shaved my hair to become a monk and am now included within the ranks of the Triple Gem; I ought to act in this manner."

To practice in this manner is not beyond one's capacity; indeed, the very act of discarding what is pleasant and adhering to what is unpleasant is precisely the means for subduing the mind of arrogance.
If arrogance arises, it obstructs the work of the Path; one must extinguish it swiftly and may not be remiss.
That which is unsuitable for a layperson is as the *Book of Rites* says: "Haughtiness must not be prolonged," and as the *I Ching* says: "The humble and humble gentleman."

One should dwell in humility to cultivate oneself; for those who have left the household life with the resolve to seek liberation, having lowered their bodies to beg for alms, how could they instead give rise to a mind of arrogance? Therefore, such a thing is improper.
The Seventh Precept on Deceit and Crookedness:
"You bhikṣus, a deceitful and crooked mind is contrary to the Way; therefore, you should make your minds upright and honest.
You should know that deceit and crookedness serve only to deceive and delude; for one who has entered the Path, such things have no place. Therefore, you all..."
One should rectify the mind, taking integrity and straightforwardness as the foundation.
One should aspire to their intent and express their words, saying: "Those whose speech is sycophantic, their minds are necessarily crooked.

Vimalakīrti said, "The straight mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)," and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, "Because the Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same path, they emerge [from it]."
Transcending birth and death is entirely due to a straightforward mind; for a crooked and deceitful mind is contrary to the mind of the Way.

Moreover, since even the gentlemen of the world value sincerity above all when dealing with those who are inherently deceitful, how could it be permissible for a bhikṣu who has entered the Path and aspires to liberation to harbor such deceit? Therefore, one should rectify the fundamental mind.
It is appropriate that one be upright and honest.
Section Three: The Division on Accomplishing the Merits of a World-Transcending Great Person (*lokottara-mahāpuruṣa*).

(The items shown in this section—such as contentment, lack of seeking, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—are all means for accomplishing world-transcending dharmas; these are what are called the learning of a great person. Therefore, it is named a "division" [of the treatise].)
First, regarding the merit of having few desires:
You bhikṣus should know that because those with many desires seek many gains, their suffering and affliction are likewise many.
Those with few desires have no seeking and no desire, and thus lack these afflictions. One should cultivate even this state of having few desires; how much more so [the other virtues]?
Having few desires can give rise to all merits. A person with few desires has no flattery or crookedness in seeking to please others, nor are they led astray by the sensory faculties.
One who practices having few desires has a mind that is serene and free from anxiety or fear;
in whatever they encounter, there is always sufficiency, and they are never lacking. Where there is one with few desires, there is *nirvāṇa*. This is called having few desires.
Those with many desires seek manifold gains; thus, their mental mechanisms move in darkness, and anxiety and fear arise unexpectedly.
Before they have attained what they seek, they suffer from the fear of not attaining it; once they have attained it, it is still insufficient to satisfy their desires.

They engage in constant scheming and plotting, with a hundredfold anxieties and deliberations—how great indeed is their suffering! Those with few desires have no affairs and do nothing; their bodies are at peace.

Because the mind is concentrated, these afflictions do not exist; yet, if one simply possesses few desires, one already attains freedom from affliction—how much more so when, through few desires, one is able to give rise to all manner of meritorious qualities!
These merits are fivefold: first, a single-mindedness free from flattery and crookedness; second, the tranquility of the sense faculties;
third, a mind free from sorrow and fear; fourth, having abundance in all undertakings; and fifth, the ultimate realization of *nirvāṇa*. This is it.
The phrase "named 'having few desires'" (*alpeccha*) is a designation based on its meaning; the following sections should be understood in this manner.
Second, the merit of contentment:
"O Bhikṣus, if you wish to be liberated from all suffering and affliction, you should contemplate contentment. The dharma of contentment is precisely..."
In places of wealth, joy, and security, those who know contentment find peace and happiness even when lying upon the bare ground;

those who lack contentment find no satisfaction even if they dwell in heaven. Those who lack contentment are poor despite their wealth, while those who possess contentment are rich despite their poverty.
Those who lack contentment are constantly dragged away by the five desires, whereas those who possess contentment are not.
That which is the object of his compassion is called contentment.
Since all sufferings arise from a lack of contentment, one who possesses contentment is a place of wealth, joy, and peace.
For one whose mind is free from deficiency due to contentment, is he not wealthy? Being without any affliction, he is truly at ease.
Is it not a pleasure? Not to pursue the perilous, the fortuitous, or the unattainable. Is it not peace and security? To lie upon the ground and yet feel at ease is because one is content;
to dwell under heaven with a mind that is dissatisfied is because one lacks contentment.

Thus, though wealthy, one may still be poor if one harbors resentment that one’s treasures are not more numerous, one’s fields and lands are not more extensive, one’s buildings are not more magnificent, or one’s rank and titles are not higher.
Generally, in whatever he undertook, his mind was never satisfied; how could this be anything other than poverty? Yet, though poor, he was rich:
as if wearing coarse linen while possessing the warmth of fox-fur robes; as if eating mugwort and dock while enjoying the excellence of rich meats and fine grain;
as if dwelling in a thatched hut while possessing the security of a grand mansion; and as if guarding a gate or striking a bell while [possessing...]
The honor and glory of being esteemed by the world far exceed what one has attained; how could this not be called wealth?

Why is this so? Because those who do not know contentment are constantly pulled about by the five desires and find themselves increasingly lacking, until they become objects of pity for those who have attained contentment.
Third, the merit of seclusion:
"O bhikṣus, those of you who desire tranquility, the unconditioned, and peace and happiness, should leave behind clamor and dwell alone in quietude.
Such persons are revered by Śakra and the devas. Therefore, you should abandon both your own group and other groups."
Dwelling alone in seclusion, one contemplates the eradication of the root of suffering; if one delights in the company of others, one will undergo manifold afflictions.

Just as a great tree that many birds flock to suffers the calamity of withering and breaking, so too those bound by worldly attachments are submerged in manifold sufferings, like an old elephant mired in mud, unable to extricate itself. This is called "separation."
The text is divided into two sections: first, the merit of remaining aloof is clarified; second, the afflictions of associating with the crowd are clarified.
This is the first section. The opening phrase indicates the fruit sought: tranquil *nirvāṇa*. Because it cuts off all discursive thoughts, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because it is free from the suffering of birth and death, it is blissful. The subsequent four phrases clarify the skillful means for cultivation, namely:
To seek pearls, one should wait for the waves to be calm; if the water is stirred, it is difficult to obtain them.

How much more so when one seeks the priceless treasure of Nirvana while dwelling in the turbid and clamorous realm of worldly toil—how could it possibly be attained? Therefore, one ought to leave the bustle and dwell in seclusion.
"Śakra" here is translated as "Capable Lord," meaning he is able to serve as the lord of the Thirty-three Heavens. [He is] revered as...
Śūnyatā-janman (Kongsheng) sat in meditative seclusion within a rocky cave while Śakra scattered flowers over him; such instances illustrate this.

Therefore, the following three lines admonish and exhort one to distance oneself from "one's own group," which refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and "other groups," which refers to followers and attendants. For those who contemplate the extinction of the root of suffering, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"The cause of all sufferings is craving; this is their very root. Next, the passage beginning with "If one delights in groups" clarifies the nature of delighting in groups.
The great tree is a metaphor for one’s own mind; the flock of birds represents oneself and others. The withering and breaking of the trees signifies the mind being afflicted by the multitude.
The elephant sinking in the mud signifies the body being submerged by the multitude.

Indeed, leaving the crowd to dwell in seclusion may appear outwardly like solitary self-benefit, yet by ceasing distraction and entering the Way, the benefit is immense. This is what is called "learning for oneself."
Because one cannot benefit others if one does not first benefit oneself, and while it is easy for others to abandon themselves, it is difficult for one to leave one's own group;
unless one has realized the fundamental source and extinguished all attachments, one will inevitably flee from peak to valley—this is something the wise must understand.
Fourth, the merit of diligence:
"O bhikṣus, if you are diligent and energetic, then no task will be difficult. Therefore, you should be diligent and energetic.
For example, even a small amount of water, if it flows constantly, can pierce through stone; yet if the mind of a practitioner repeatedly becomes lax and desists,"
For example, it is like drilling for fire: if one stops before the heat has been generated, although one wishes to obtain fire, it will be difficult to find.

This is called diligence (*vīrya*). There are two aspects of diligence: the aspect of phenomena (*dharma*) and the aspect of principle (*artha*). The phenomenon is the diligent cultivation of practice in every thought-moment;

the principle is the emptiness and quiescence in every thought-moment. Even water flowing without ceasing can pierce stone; this serves as a metaphor for the accomplishment achieved through diligence, such as drilling for fire.
The analogy that fire cannot be obtained by counting breaths illustrates that laziness leads to no accomplishment.
Regarding the merit of the fivefold mindfulness:
O bhikṣus, in seeking a virtuous friend or seeking virtuous protection and assistance, nothing is equal to non-forgetfulness of mindfulness. If there is such forgetfulness...
The thieves of the various afflictions cannot enter one who possesses mindfulness; therefore, you should always collect the mind and keep it within.
If mindfulness is lost, all merits are lost; if the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, even if one enters among the thieves of the five desires, one will not be harmed.
It is like wearing armor when entering battle, whereby one has nothing to fear. This is called "unfailing mindfulness."

The "knowledgeable friend who instructs" is the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who provides guidance; the "knowledgeable friend who protects and assists" is the spiritual friend who provides external protection.
There is nothing like the practice of non-forgetfulness (*asmṛti*). While these two types of friends depend on others, non-forgetfulness depends upon oneself.
Even if one possesses the former two, if one’s own right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) is lost, what is the use? Therefore, one must constantly maintain this vigilance at all times.
If one constantly causes right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) to be present, then all the thieves of affliction (*kleśa*) will have no way to enter.
Regarding "gathering the mind within," the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately gather it back and abide in right mindfulness.
As for this right mindfulness, one should know that there are only minds and no external objects; furthermore, even this mind itself is non-existent.
That the self-characteristics cannot be apprehended moment by moment is precisely this point.

To lose mindfulness is to lose all merits, like entering a battle without armor so that the enemy may find an opening. When mindfulness is strong, the thieves of the passions cannot cause harm, like wearing armor into battle and being entirely without fear.
Regarding the merit of the six dhyānas:

"O bhikṣus, if you collect the mind, the mind will be in meditative concentration. Because the mind is in concentration, one is able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of phenomena in the world.
Therefore, you should always diligently practice all forms of concentration; for those who attain concentration..."
The mind is then undistracted, just as a household that cherishes water skillfully maintains its dikes and ponds. The practitioner is likewise;
for the sake of the water of wisdom, they skillfully cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) so that it does not leak away. This is called concentration (*samādhi*).

"Collecting the mind leads to concentration" refers back to the preceding discussion on non-forgetfulness; it means that because the mind does not wander due to non-forgetfulness, one attains concentration.
"Being able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena" clarifies the fruit of achieving concentration:
through mental stability, clarity is like the purity of the ocean, wherein all things appear as reflections. "Various concentrations" refers to the various... [text ends]
In the sūtras and śāstras, phenomena and principle differ, as do the Great and Small Vehicles; one should diligently practice according to what is appropriate for one's own faculties.

This is like a person learning archery: after a long time, they naturally hit the mark. An embankment is formed by piling up earth to prevent water from leaking; if there were no embankment, the water would leak away.
Likewise, if there is no meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*) will be lost. As the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Unobstructed purity."
Since pure wisdom arises entirely from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), you should cultivate concentration.
Seventh, regarding the merit of wisdom:
O bhikṣus, if you possess wisdom, you will be free from greedy attachment; you must constantly examine yourselves so as not to allow any lapse.
This is how one attains liberation within my Dharma; were it otherwise, one would be neither a seeker of the Way nor a layperson, and thus have no name at all.
True wisdom is a sturdy ship for crossing the ocean of old age, sickness, and death;
it is a great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; and it is the excellent medicine for all who are ill. It is the axe that fells... [the tree of affliction].
It is the sharp axe for the tree of afflictions; therefore, you should increase your own merit through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
If a person possesses the illumination of wisdom, even though they possess only physical eyes, they are one who sees clearly; such a person is truly wise.
The text is divided into three sections: first, the Dharma; second, the analogy; and third, the exhortation. This is the first section.
"Sentient beings are attached everywhere" because they lack wisdom. If one possessed wisdom, there would be no attachment.

Because a bhikṣu practices the dharma of seclusion, he should always examine himself with a mind of wisdom regarding what is true and what is false within both the mundane and supramundane realms. Is it real? Is it illusory? Is it...?
If one ensures that what should be done is done and what should not be done is not done, so that no error occurs, then one will certainly attain liberation within the Buddha-dharma.

Otherwise, the mind will be darkened; being neither the form of a practitioner of the Way—since the hair has already been shaved and dyed—nor a layperson, being held by neither side, what can such a person be called?
Regarding "true wisdom" below, the metaphor of true wisdom serves to distinguish [it from false wisdom].
It is not worldly wisdom or eloquence that constitutes true *prajñā*.

The metaphors of the boat, the lamp, the medicine, and the axe collectively illustrate that actual wisdom possesses the merit of crossing over birth and death, destroying ignorance, curing the diseases of the mind, and felling the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Therefore, [the text] below exhorts the cultivation of the three types of wisdom: hearing is called "reaching the ear," reflecting is called "investigating the principle," and practice is called "arousing action."
Cultivating wisdom derived from hearing is like an overturned vessel that cannot receive water; wisdom derived from reflection is like a leaking vessel that loses what it receives;
and wisdom derived from cultivation is like a defiled vessel that, though neither leaking nor losing its contents, is so foul as to be unusable.
These three must be fully possessed—like a vessel that is upright, intact, and pure—before they can be put to use.
Wisdom is the light inherently present within one's own mind;
because it is obscured by afflictions, it cannot manifest, and thus one must rely on the three types of wisdom to augment it, so that when defilements are exhausted, the light may arise.
That the physical eye sees clearly is due to the predominance of mental wisdom.
8. Ultimate Merit:
"O bhikṣus, if you engage in various forms of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), your minds will become distracted; though you have left the household life, you have not yet attained liberation.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you must urgently abandon the conceptual proliferation of a distracted mind if you desire to attain the bliss of tranquility (*śānti*)."
One should simply skillfully extinguish the affliction of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); this is called "non-proliferation.
There are two types of conceptual proliferation: first, that which gives rise to proliferation regarding the true principle, such as the four propositions and hundred negations;
second, that which gives rise to proliferation regarding worldly affairs, such as jesting and sarcasm. Quiescence is precisely *nirvāṇa*. It is said:
To attain the bliss of the quiescence of Nirvana, one must necessarily still and unify the mind;

if the mind is distracted, how could it possibly be attained? Therefore, one must skillfully extinguish the affliction of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), for the affliction of conceptual proliferation is itself a distracted mind.

Section Four: Manifesting the Ultimate Profound Merit (The heading of this section indicates that from beginning to end, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma and benefiting of sentient beings have all been brought to ultimate perfection; therefore, it is so named).
"You bhikṣus, regarding all merits, you should always maintain a single mind and abandon all negligence, as if avoiding enemies and thieves."
The benefits taught by the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One have all been fully accomplished; you should simply practice them with diligence.
Whether in the mountains, in empty marshes, beneath trees, or in secluded and quiet rooms, contemplate the Dharma you have received and do not let it be lost.
You must always exert yourselves and cultivate it with vigor, lest you die in vain and later come to regret it.
I am like a skilled physician who diagnoses the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether it is taken or not is not the fault of the physician.
Again, I am like a good guide who leads people onto the right path; that they hear the instructions but do not act upon them is not the fault of the guide.
"All merits" refers to the aforementioned few desires, contentment, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
"Single-mindedness" means practicing all these merits with a unified mind, without giving rise to dualistic thoughts.

"Abandoning all negligence as one would flee from enemies and thieves" means that because enemies and thieves plunder wealth and take life, while negligence fosters evil and destroys goodness, it is fitting to distance oneself from it, O World-Honored One.

"Whatever has been taught is already complete" means that from the beginning at the Deer Park until the end at the Bahudā River, all the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle taught in the interim are now fully consummated; nothing remains to be left out.
Those who come after need only rely on these teachings and practice them diligently. Mountain clefts, empty marshes, beneath trees, and quiet chambers are all suitable places for this.
Regarding the place of practice, one should be mindful of the teachings received so as not to let them be forgotten.
This is because sentient beings of the desire realm abandon stillness and rush toward movement; although they receive the teachings, it is like a leaking vessel, causing much to be lost.
Therefore, the Buddha has them dwell in quietude and seclusion to be mindful of the teachings received. Once the teachings received are clear, the practices one cultivates can be perfected.
To advance toward death only to die empty-handed and later regret it—this is because those whose minds seek the tranquility of stillness are nonetheless entangled by the realm of desire;

their lives pass in a daze, and when death arrives, they are struck with remorse. Once the bite has been taken, what can be done? A wise person once said: "There was a Chan master of Ye and Luo whose fame spread across the rivers and seas.
When he stayed, people from the four quarters looked up to him like clouds; when he moved, hundreds and thousands followed him in droves, creating a deep and thunderous roar."

What benefit is there in this world for those who all feel regret at the moment of death? The parable of the skilled physician prescribing medicine illustrates how the Dharma is taught to destroy evil;

the parable of the good guide leading people illustrates how the Dharma is taught to give rise to goodness. Whether one takes and practices [the medicine] or not is the fault of sentient beings alone;
the Buddha does not intervene. Alas! His words of sincere blood-and-tears are thus repeated with such earnestness, yet it is we ourselves who have failed him.
Alas, how tragic it is that the Buddha’s grace has instead brought about this transgression! V.
Manifesting the Section on the Certainty of Entry into Realization (This section examines whether the assembly harbors doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths;
it is so named because it seeks to ensure their certain entry into realization, free from any state of hesitation).
"If you have any doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and the rest, you may ask about them quickly;
do not harbor uncertainty or fail to seek a resolution. At that time, the World-Honored One made this proclamation three times, yet no one asked a question.
Why was this? It was because the assembly had no doubts. Then, Ānanda, observing the minds of the assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, [the moon...]"
One cannot make the hot sun cold; so too, the Buddha has taught the Four Noble Truths, which cannot be made otherwise.
The Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure. Accumulation is truly the cause, and there is no other cause.

When suffering ceases, it is because the cause has ceased; because the cause has ceased, the fruit ceases. The Path for the cessation of suffering is truly the Path, and there is no other path, World-Honored One.
These bhikṣus were free from doubt and hesitation regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Since the Four Noble Truths—the dharmas to be known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated—are received equally by all, whether great or small, he urged them to question him.

As for those who were already without doubt, he [addressed] the assembly as a whole, for they had all attended various assemblies where the teachings on arising and ceasing, non-arising, and the immeasurable had been revealed.
Since [the Buddha] has already fully realized non-action and so forth, there is no longer any room for doubt.
Although the Great Assembly has no doubts and the Buddha surely knows this, he nonetheless asks three times out of his boundless great compassion for all beings.
Aniruddha—also known as Anuruddha—is translated here as "Wish-Fulfilling. In the past, he offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha.
He was so named because he had received the retribution of having his every wish fulfilled for ninety-one kalpas.
At that time, as the foremost among the assembly, he observed the minds of the multitude and addressed the Buddha, saying: "The natures of heat and cold in the sun and moon may perhaps be altered;
however, the principle of the Buddha’s true words can never change. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that within the three realms there are twenty-five states of suffering."
That which exists in reality is indeed suffering; it cannot be made into pleasure. Accumulation (*samudaya*) is truly the cause of the fruit of suffering.

Apart from the views and afflictions (*kleśa*), there is no other cause capable of producing suffering. The cessation of the fruit of suffering is precisely the cessation of its cause. Because the cause ceases, the fruit ceases;
the simultaneous cessation of both cause and fruit is the true Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The path for the cessation of suffering is truly real.
Apart from the path of morality, concentration, and wisdom, there is no other path capable of extinguishing suffering;
this Lohita answered according to the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing realized by the Śrāvakas, yet in reality, all the disciples have already attained certainty regarding non-arising,
the immeasurable, and so forth, and are beyond further doubt.

Those who had first entered the Dharma, upon hearing what the Buddha taught, immediately attained deliverance; it was as if seeing the path at once by the flash of lightning in the night.
Those who had already accomplished what was to be done and had crossed the ocean of suffering merely thought:
"How swift is the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One! Although Ānanda spoke these words, everyone in the assembly fully realized the Four Noble Truths.
The World-Honored One, desiring that this great assembly all attain firmness regarding the meaning of the Truths, further preached for the sake of the multitude out of his great compassion. Herein,
the sūtra-narrator describes how those who had not yet completed their tasks wept tears like rain from heaven and gods, while Ānanda was filled with sorrow.
Among these types, those who first enter the Dharma and attain liberation upon hearing what the Buddha teaches are like Ābhadra and his peers;
those who have already accomplished what was to be done and have crossed the ocean of suffering in the three realms of existence are like the various Arhats.

Because the visions of these two types of spiritual capacities are not the same, each harbors doubts. This is entirely due to their failure to comprehend that the Tathāgata’s teaching is a single, unified event.
Although Lokeśvara had thus explained the principle of ultimate permanence and non-extinction, the World-Honored One,
out of his inexhaustible great compassion and desiring that all beings attain the ultimately firm and steadfast mind, again resolved their doubts for the assembly, saying:
"You bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress. Even if I were to remain in the world for an eon, this assembly would still eventually perish;
that an assembly should not part is ultimately impossible. The Dharma for self-benefit and the benefit of others is fully complete. If I were to remain much longer, it would bring no further benefit.
Those among gods and humans who were to be delivered have all already been delivered; as for those not yet delivered..."

Furthermore, having already established the causes and conditions for crossing over, from this day forward, if my disciples practice this in succession, then the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata will be eternally present and never perish.
Therefore, you should know that all worlds are impermanent and that every meeting must end in separation;
do not harbor grief or distress. Since the nature of the world is thus, you should diligently apply yourselves with vigor to seek liberation early.
Wisdom illuminates and extinguishes the darkness of all delusions; the world is truly precarious and fragile, possessing nothing that is firm or enduring.

Now that I have attained this extinction, it is like being cured of a malignant disease. This is a sinful thing to be abandoned, merely designated by the false name of "body," which dwells within the great ocean of old age, sickness, birth, and death.
What wise person, having eliminated it as one would slay a hostile enemy, would not rejoice?

The text is divided into two sections: first, the resolution of doubts; second, a further demonstration of the characteristics of impermanence. Now, for the first section, the assembly: since there is assembly, there must necessarily be dispersal.
This has two parts: first, the assembly and dispersal of teacher and disciple; second, the assembly and dispersal of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"Those who fully possess the dharmas of self-benefit and benefiting others" refers to those who have attained the fruits [of the path] and have delivered sentient beings. "Abiding for a long time."
There are also two reasons why [the Buddha’s] remaining would be of no benefit: first, the Buddhas abide in the world solely for the purpose of teaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings;

since that task is already accomplished, it would be of no further benefit. Second, if the Buddha were to remain for a long time, sentient beings would not conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter.

Regarding those who have not yet been delivered but for whom the conditions for deliverance have been established: this refers to those who, upon seeing the Buddha, have already [set the cause for their liberation].
I preach the Dharma so that those who have not yet seen the Buddha may plant seeds within them;
my disciples shall successively transmit it so that it remains uninterrupted. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body abiding eternally in the world without perishing.
Why, then, should you feel grief and distress? For this reason, I again demonstrate the characteristics of impermanence below, first showing them as follows:
The world is impermanent; following this, I now cite myself as proof. When one sees the body persist, one is delighted and does not grow weary of it, for thus craving arises.
When one sees the body perish, one is grieved and does not rejoice, for thus one seeks to avoid death. These are the actions of the foolish. The wise are the opposite;
therefore it is said that their joy is like being cured of a malignant disease or like slaying a vengeful enemy—this joy is evident.
Question: "The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body; it is fundamentally unborn and thus neither arises nor perishes, nor does it perish now.
Why is it that the various afflictions you have just described are exactly like those of ordinary beings—blazing with arising and perishing? Answer:
"It is because sentient beings delusively identify the four great elements as their bodies. From this, they give rise to delusions and create karma, sinking into the ocean of suffering."

Because one is able to attain Buddhahood and has already demonstrated that it is identical to the human dharma, the text speaks to the extreme gravity of its faults and takes the attainment of cessation as joy;
this is what is meant by "by the cessation of this form, one obtains eternal form."

Section Seven: On Being Free from the Various Self-Natures and Purified Non-Self (This section is titled as such because the World-Honored One has distanced himself from the various self-natures of the world and entered the pure non-self of *nirvāṇa*;
this non-self is precisely the True Self).
"O bhikṣus, you should always with a single mind diligently seek the path out of the world; [regard] all phenomena of the world, whether moving or unmoving..."
"All these are signs of decay and instability; you should now desist and say no more.
The time is passing and I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; this is my final instruction."
The "path leading out from birth and death" refers precisely to the various Dharma-gates shown above.
"All worlds" is a general designation for the three realms: the desire realm of movement, and the form and formless realms of non-movement. "Decay" refers to impermanence;
as it is said regarding *nirvāṇa*, "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. "Insecurity" refers to oppression.
The *Fa-hua jing* (Lotus Sūtra) states: "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house.
This refers to the time when [the night] was about to pass, which occurred at midnight. That it did not pass signifies the Middle Way.
These are my final instructions—words of urgent and earnest admonition that you should always keep in mind and never hastily forget. From this point on, remain settled.
However, upon entering the nirvana of intrinsic purity, both body and speech are completely exhausted, for its intrinsic nature is signless and free from sound and form.
If this is so, why visit [the Buddha] in person? To address this, the Sūtra states: "It is precisely this."
