The Cautionary Admonition of Chan Master Dayuan of Mount Gui.
Mount Gui is located in Ningxiang County of Changsha Prefecture; it spans approximately one hundred and forty *li* in circumference, and the Gui River originates there. Therefore...
The Master’s name was Lingyou; "Dachuan" (Great Circle) was his posthumous title. He was a native of Changxi in Fuzhou and belonged to the Zhao clan.
At the age of fifteen, he entered the monastic order under Vinaya Master Fachang of Jianshan Temple in his home prefecture.

He subsequently went to Longxing Temple in Hangzhou to study the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. At twenty-three, he traveled to Jiangxi to visit Baizhang, who was the sole successor of Mazu.
Having been granted permission, the Master entered the room and stood in attendance. Baizhang asked, "Who is your teacher? The Master replied, "I am so-and-so.
Baizhang said, "Is there fire in the brazier? The Master poked it and said, "There is no fire in the brazier.

Baizhang rose from his seat, poked deeply into the embers, and finding a small spark, he held it up to show the Master, saying, "You say there is no fire—what about this? At this, the Master attained awakening and bowed in gratitude. Afterwards...
When the Vinaya Master Sima selected Mount Gui as his dwelling place, the Master (Baizhang) was serving as the head cook (*dianzuo*).

The Master [Baizhang] commanded that the Master [Huangbo] go to reside there as abbot, entrusting him with these words: "My karmic conditions for transformation lie here at the sublime site of Mount Gui;

you shall dwell there, succeed my lineage, and extensively deliver future students. When Huailin heard this, he said: "I, this humble person, am unworthily occupying the position of Head Cook (*shangzuo dian*)."
The Abbot asked, "How can you maintain the position of abbot? Linji said, "If I can deliver a phrase that transcends the ordinary when facing the assembly, I shall serve as abbot.
The Abbot then pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "You must not call this a 'water pitcher'; what would you call it?
Linji replied, "I cannot call it a 'wooden gourd' either. The Abbot turned to his attendant, and Linji kicked over the pitcher and immediately departed.
Baizhang laughed and said, "The First Seat has lost the mountain. The Master then went there.
The mountain was steep and precipitous, utterly devoid of human habitation; monkeys were his companions and acorns and chestnuts his food.
After five or seven years, Daman An arrived from Baizhang accompanied by several monks to assist him. Thereupon, those who studied Chan began to gather like the spokes of a wheel.

Subsequently, the lineage of Master Yangshan and his disciples further flourished through their teaching and chanting, and their reputation spread widely; the world came to recognize them as the founding masters of the Guiyang and Dayang schools.

Observing that practitioners were becoming indolent and that this was gradually leading to corruption, he composed the "Jingsce" (Exhortation). This work became widely circulated throughout the monastic communities;
as for the term "jingsce," it is like rousing someone from a deep sleep to awaken them, or like [reinvigorating] a horse that has grown weary.
He exhorts them to advance because sentient beings sleep through the great night of birth and death, becoming indolent in cultivating the path of the Dharma.
Thus, the Master’s composition of this admonition may truly be called a manifestation of his sincere compassion for those in distress.
Should they fail to awaken despite the warning or fail to progress despite the exhortation, they are merely self-indulgent and self-abandoning.

The first major section is divided into two parts: the prose text and the inscription. The inscription is further divided into five sections: (1) demonstrating the great afflictions of the physical body;
(2) rectifying the abuses prevalent among those who have left the household life; (3) clarifying the true cause for leaving the household life; (4) showing the path for entering the Way;
and (5) concluding with earnest exhortations. This is the first [section].
Now, one bound by karma receives a body and cannot escape the burden of form.

"Karma" refers to the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—created in the past; "receiving a body" refers to the ripening consciousness (the eighth consciousness) receiving the present body as it is bound by prior karma.
Karma belongs to the cause, while the body belongs to the effect, because the cause exists [and thus brings about the result].
Because there is a distinction between good and evil, their fruits differ as suffering and joy; the physical burdens are birth, old age, sickness, and death.
This is what Laozi meant when he said, "I have a great affliction: that I have a body."
This physical body is received from one's parents and is brought into being through the convergence of various conditions.
This passage generally explains the reception of the body; since this body is formed from the essence and blood of the parents, it is called "the inherited body" (*yiti*).

As for the "various conditions," these refer to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): first, one relies on the internal four great elements to be born, and subsequently, one relies on the external four...
Because they nourish one another on a grand scale, they are said to "jointly accomplish" [the body].
Although the four great elements support one another, they are constantly in mutual opposition.
Hereafter, the specific explanation of the physical burden regarding the support of the four great elements means that the four great elements mutually support one another.
The meaning is as follows: it is like water encountering fire and not becoming cold, or fire encountering water and not becoming parched.
That which is said to be "constantly in opposition" refers to the natures of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), whose ascending and descending, movement and stillness, are mutually contradictory.
Since they possess both the function of mutual support and the harm of mutual opposition, there arise the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Impermanence, old age, and sickness do not set an appointment with anyone; one may exist in the morning and perish in the evening, changing worlds in a single *kṣaṇa*.
"Not setting an appointment" means arriving suddenly and unexpectedly; "changing worlds in a *kṣaṇa*" means being separated from this life in an instant.
For example, spring frost and morning dew vanish in an instant; how could trees on a riverbank or vines by a well endure for long?
These four metaphors prove that spring frost is easily melted and morning dew is easily dried, as is commonly known to the world.
Regarding "trees on a riverbank," this refers to those that are easily toppled. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "For example, if a tree standing on a steep riverbank encounters..."
A violent wind will inevitably cause one to fall; human beings are likewise thus. When approaching the perilous brink of old age, once the wind of death arrives, there is no power to remain.
"The well-creeper" refers to its being easily severed. As the Sūtra says:
"It is as if a person were walking through a vast wilderness amidst a great conflagration and being pursued by a mad elephant; seeing a withered well, upon which stands a tree..."
The vine is the person; the vine is suspended in a well where, below, dwell three venomous dragons and four poisonous snakes.
Furthermore, black and white rats gnaw at the vine on all four sides, while bees with venom surround it. There is a small amount of honey dripping into the mouth;

because of greed for this honey, one consequently forgets the suffering. The vast wilderness is a metaphor for the triple world (triloka); the tree is a metaphor for the body; and the vine is a metaphor for [life].
The life-faculty is likened to an elephant; impermanence is likened to a murderous demon; the two rats are likened to the sun and moon; the well is likened to the Yellow Springs (the underworld);

and the three dragons are likened to the three poisons. The four snakes are likened to the four great elements, and honey is likened to the five desires. Because one becomes obsessed with the desires for wealth, beauty, and the like, one consequently forgets the great suffering of birth and death.
Thought after thought passes in rapid succession; in a single kṣaṇa, one breath shifts and one is already in the next life.
How can you remain so complacent and let time pass in vain? These four lines summarize the preceding text: the transformations of birth and death are extremely swift;
one must advance in virtue in a timely manner and must not sit idly by waiting for decline. "Kṣaṇa" refers to the shortest possible duration of time; this is precisely what issues forth as a warning.

The intention behind Zhe’s words is that the opening of the *Kaishuai* (Awakening the Heavy) immediately indicates that those who suffer from heaviness of body do so because this is the very root of suffering.

If one does not understand this meaning and instead speaks at random about leaving home to study the Way, asserting that every movement and action is nothing but the livelihood of a skull, such a person is merely sufficient to increase the karma of birth and death; how could they ever enter the Way?
Second, as for the abuses prevalent among those who have left home:

their parents no longer receive succulent delicacies; they are abandoned by their six kin; they cannot bring peace to the state or the clan; their family estate is suddenly lost; their lineage is severed;

they are distantly separated from their hometowns; they shave their heads and take precepts from a teacher; internally, they diligently cultivate the merit of self-restraint and mindfulness; externally, they propagate...
The virtue of non-contention transcends the mundane world, aspiring toward liberation.

This clearly elucidates the excellence of the intent behind renouncing the world and, by contrast, rectifying its prevailing abuses. "Six relations" refers to the kinship of paternal uncles, brothers, sons, and grandsons;

"family estate" refers to the sudden abandonment of such affairs by those who have renounced the world. "Lineage" refers to the successor; for one who has renounced the world, the family estate is suddenly cast aside.

And there was no one to continue his lineage; "mian" means distant. One thousand two hundred and fifty households constitute a *xiang* (district), and five hundred households constitute a *dang* (village).

"Kernian" means being able to maintain mindfulness; as the *Shangshu* says, "Only the madman who can maintain mindfulness becomes a sage," which is precisely what the *Śāsanānuśāsanī* (The Bequeathed Teaching) refers to as "not forgetting mindfulness.
"Non-contention" (*araṇa*) is the name for the Saṃgha, as it is in harmony with all things.
Among humans, one should not give rise to contentious debate.

Now, those born between the two polarities [Heaven and Earth] ought to filially support their parents, love and respect their six relations, bring peace and order to the state, and foster harmony within their local communities; furthermore, they should prosper their family affairs and inherit the ancestral sacrifices—these are indeed what they must do.
Yet now, you all abandon these entirely and fail to practice them, choosing instead to shave your hair, disfigure your appearance, and receive instruction from a master.
Those who receive the Dharma desire to exert themselves inwardly and propagate it outwardly, hoping to escape the net of worldly dust to repay their parents and support their six kin.
Since the common practices of the secular world are false and unreal, binding one to birth and death with no foreseeable end, they willingly abandon them;
this is the fundamental purpose of leaving home and becoming a renunciant.

How is it that as soon as one has ascended to the level of the precepts, one immediately declares, "I am a bhikṣu," yet regarding what is required by the donors for consumption—such as the property of the Sangha—one fails to reflect upon its origin, claiming instead that it is naturally right to consume it;
having finished eating, they gather together in a noisy clamor, speaking only of various worldly matters.
Thus, in their pursuit of pleasure for a time, they do not realize that this pleasure is the cause of suffering.
"Why, then, do you instead reproach him? This refers to the words of the *Upasampadā-śikṣāpada*.

"Reflecting on the source from which it comes" refers to the Buddha’s regulation that a bhikṣu, upon receiving food, must perform five reflections (*pañca saṃjñā*): first, calculate the labor expended and measure the distance from its source;

second, reflect upon one's own virtue to determine whether one is worthy of the offering; third, guard the mind against faults, making the abandonment of greed and other afflictions the primary principle.
The primary purpose of excellent medicine is to treat the withered body; the fifth reason for accepting this food is for the sake of accomplishing the Path.
Now, you do not reflect at all, thinking only: "I am a bhikṣu; it is the natural law that I ought to receive the constant offerings of the donors.
A "single period" (*eka-kāla*) is merely a way of saying "for a time," yet you rush after pleasure, gathering together in noisy clamor—such pleasures are the cause of suffering.
This means that the pleasure of indulgence before one's eyes is sufficient to invoke the bitter fruits of future retribution;
as the ancients said, "A single grain of rice offered in faith is as heavy as Mount Sumeru. If one does not understand the Way, will they not still have to wear fur and carry horns?
Should they not stand in awe?
Throughout kalpas past, I have followed after the dust of sensory objects without ever reflecting upon them; time has slipped away and years have been wasted.

My enjoyments have been abundant and my gains and benefits have been thick and rich, yet for many years I have had no intention of renouncing them. My accumulations have grown ever more numerous as I have maintained this illusory physical form.
The four lines beginning with "In past kalpas" mean that they lack the power of self-reflection and instead follow along with sensory objects,
letting the years and months pass in vain. The six lines beginning with "Enjoyment" mean that they are greedily attached to sensory gratification,
amassing offerings and profits to maintain their illusory bodies.
The Teacher has issued a command to exhort the bhikṣus to advance on the Path and adorn themselves; yet, these three things are always insufficient, and many people indulge in them without ceasing.
As days pass and months come, suddenly their hair turns white.
This follows from the previous discussion regarding abundant enjoyments, stating that a bhikṣu should not be like this.

"Advancing in the Way" and "studying the Way" refer to the requisites for adorning and sustaining the body. The "three things that are not to be satisfied" are clothing, food, and sleep; these three should not be pursued to excess.
Clothing is taken only to cover the body, not for its ornamental finery; food is taken only to sustain life, not out of greed for exquisite flavors.
One sleeps to relieve fatigue, but must not allow the mind to run wild; this is because one fears being deluded and obscured by it, which would hinder and ruin one's spiritual practice.
Confucius said, "In eating, do not seek satiety; in dwelling, do not seek comfort. This is precisely that same intent.
People of the world do not set their will upon the Way, yet they indulge excessively in these three things, savoring them without ceasing and busily seeking fulfillment day after day.
That last month came and I did not realize that old age had suddenly arrived—is this not due to the errors of these three?

Those of later learning have not yet heard the essential meaning; they ought to consult widely with those who possess prior knowledge. Otherwise, one might suppose that leaving the household life is merely for the sake of seeking food and clothing.
"Principle and intent" refers to the principle and intent of renouncing the household life. The intent of renunciation lies in seeing one's nature and delivering sentient beings;
if those of later generations have not yet heard of this, they ought to inquire extensively of those who are already advanced and rely upon them to seek it out.
Since you have neither heard of it nor inquired about it, do you suppose that those who renounce the world value nothing but seeking food and clothing? How can this be so extreme?
This is an error.
The Buddha first established the Vinaya to initiate the unenlightened, providing rules and decorum as pure as ice and snow;

it restrains transgressions through observance and action, binding the novice mind with subtle regulations to reform all vulgar abuses. Yet, I have never once had the fortune to participate in such a *vinaya* assembly.
How can one distinguish the definitive meaning of the Supreme Vehicle? It is a pity that a lifetime passes in vain; once regret sets in, it is difficult to pursue.
This refers to those who do not study the Vinaya. As for the Vinaya, it is the initial gateway to the Three Trainings; if one does not study it, by what means could one advance upon the Path?
To say it "initiates and awakens the ignorant" means that the Vinaya established by the Buddha is that which first initiates and awakens [the practitioner].

Regarding their state of ignorance: those who have only recently left the household life are mentally and physically obscured; knowing only indulgence and lacking restraint, how can they guard themselves?

The "abstaining from transgressions" (*śīla*) and the "performing of violations" refer to the precepts established by the Tathāgata, such as the five categories and seven groups, which serve to bind and constrain those with a beginner's mind. As for the subtle and minute regulations...

The rules of conduct (*vinaya*) and dignified demeanor (*īryāpatha*) are intended to reform all vulgar and corrupt practices. The *vinaya* is the seat of the Dharma and the workshop of the discipline;
I have never yet been privileged to attend it—meaning I have never even entered the gate of the workshop of the discipline—and thus have merely joined the pure assembly by right of excess.

If I have not even joined as an excess, it is clear that my nature is rustic and uncultivated. Since I do not yet know the practical application of the study of the *vinaya*, how could I possibly understand its higher principles?
How can one who merely rides upon the profound principle truly discern it? To pass through a lifetime in vain, even if regret arises later, what can be done?
Alas, how lamentable!
Having never applied oneself to the teachings and principles, and having no means to realize the profound Way, one reaches old age with long-standing seniority, yet remains empty-handed within.
"With a haughty mind, they refuse to associate with virtuous friends, knowing only how to be arrogant.
This speaks of their failure to practice the teaching. Now, the teaching is a bright mirror that illuminates the mind;
if one does not practice it, by what means shall the mind attain awakening? The final four lines then reveal the faults of failing to practice the teaching and of not associating with the virtuous.
This friend displays a haughty mind born of an empty stomach; he knows only to be arrogant and to rely on his seniority in years.
Unfamiliar with the Vinaya, he lacks all restraint; he speaks loudly and in high tones, uttering words without moderation, showing no respect for the elders, the equals, or the juniors.
He is no different from a gathering of Brahmins, making noise with his bowl and departing before the meal is finished.

Your monastic character is utterly lacking; you are restless whether sitting or rising, disturbing the minds of others with your every movement, and you do not maintain even the slightest rules or minor points of decorum.
How can you constrain yourself? Those who come after you, the new students, have no one to emulate.
As soon as they observe your conduct, they say, "I am a mountain monk. Yet I have never heard such a thing in the Buddha's teachings; your practice is consistently coarse and crude in spirit.

This describes the faults of one who is unaccustomed to the Vinaya. The Vinaya is that which binds and restrains the beginner's mind; since one is not conversant with the Vinaya, how can there be restraint?
To speak with loud voices and without hesitation is to utter words without measure, for such speech issues forth what is contrary to the Dharma and lacks self-discipline.
It is to show no respect toward the senior, middle, or junior seats, thereby disregarding the order of honor between the noble and the lowly.
The Brahmins are non-Buddhists. The *Śīla-sūtra* says:
"In my Buddha-dharma, those who have received the precepts first sit in front, and those who have received them later sit behind; do not sit without order like the foolish non-Buddhists.
Those who make noise with their bowls and alms-basins do not consider the suffering of hungry ghosts. Those who rise first after the meal cause the entire assembly to startle."
To act with such discordant conduct is contrary to ritual propriety and is not the essence of a monk. To be agitated and restless in rising and sitting disturbs the thoughts of others;
"tōngzhū" (忪諸) describes a state of coarse haste and a lack of adherence to rules. This concludes the summary of these various faults. "Vigilance" (*juecha*) is like a whip of admonition.
When I speak of "mountain monks" (*shanseng*), I mean those monks of the wilds who do not recognize etiquette; this is because they reject counsel and merely patch up their own faults.
The language used to criticize them is coarse and vulgar, such as using loud voices and high-pitched speech.
Such views arise because beginners are indolent, gluttonous, and negligent; as time passes, they become increasingly rustic and uncultivated.
This summarizes the reasons for the two aforementioned faults: those who are indolent have inferior resolve; those who are lazy are remiss in their efforts;
the gluttonous crave food; the covetous crave wealth; and those who follow the flow lack any sense of urgency or aspiration, merely following along with the crowd and the pack.
It is because these types begin with such an attitude from the outset that they eventually breed a state of neglect and wildness. This process unfolds through the gradual passage of time.

Reflecting upon this state of mind, I am unaware that I have become so decrepit and senile that I face a wall whenever confronted by matters. When junior students come to inquire, I have no words to guide or lead them;
even when I do speak, it does not touch upon the classical scriptures. Should they speak lightly, I immediately rebuke them for their lack of decorum, and thus anger and resentment arise within me.
Regarding those who are ignorant of language:

it is said that such people, being unacquainted with the teachings and the Vinaya and having no application of mind, will find their suffering when old age, sickness, and death arrive beyond words to describe.
This clarifies the suffering of old age; "lóngzhòng xíng bùjìn" (limping along, unable to advance) describes the appearance of the face.
The wall-like speech of one who knows nothing refers to the four subsequent lines, all of which concern the affairs of ignorance.
As for "being slighted" by the following four lines, it means that when one is treated with contempt and fails to recognize one's own fault, one instead stirs up anger;
"the words encompassing the multitude" means that the words spoken pervasively involve others and stir the thoughts of the masses.
One morning, lying ill upon my bed, I was beset by a multitude of sufferings that oppressed me from dawn until dusk.

My mind was filled with agitation as I contemplated the path ahead—vast and obscure, with no knowledge of where it might lead. It was only then that I first realized my transgressions; digging a well when already thirsty, what is the use?
I lamented that I had not practiced in advance earlier in life, and that in my later years I had committed many faults.

This refers to one whose body is entangled and oppressed by the suffering of illness—the great sickness having come upon them and manifold sufferings arising in succession—not merely of a single kind.
At such a time, being at the very threshold of death, the delusions of a lifetime have already ceased and vigorous ambitions have turned to ash.
One reflects morning and night with a heart filled with trepidation, not knowing what lies ahead.
"How is the path ahead?"—this describes a state of confusion, agitation, and terror regarding the five destinies (*pañcagati*) that lie before one.

"When about to die, one regrets one's past transgressions" means that it is like digging a well when already thirsty; what can possibly be achieved then? The two lines beginning with "I regret" are words of repentance for one's past errors.

At the moment of departure, one is distracted, terrified, and filled with panic; like a bird flying through a tattered silk veil, the conscious mind follows its karma, as if a debtor being dragged by the strongest creditor.
The mental continuum is manifold, yet it falls wherever the weight is greatest. The demon of impermanence slays without ceasing for even a single thought-moment;
life cannot be prolonged, and time cannot be waited for. Within the three realms of existence—humans, devas, and asuras—one cannot escape this fate; such is the nature of receiving a body.
This does not refer to the duration of kalpas;
rather, it speaks of the suffering of death, meaning that in the absence of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one must meekly submit to the gateway of death.

The phrases "flitting about" and "startled and frantic" describe a state of sudden urgency and panic. Regarding the two lines concerning the "piercing of the gauze and the flight of the sparrow," the *Saptakumārikā-sūtra* states: "A sparrow came and entered... [and so forth].
A jar has its mouth covered with gauze; when the gauze is pierced, a sparrow flies away. Consciousness follows karma as the sparrow flies away.
The sparrow is a metaphor for the *ālayavijñāna*, the jar is a metaphor for the body, and the gauze is a metaphor for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

This means that once the life-faculty of the present aggregate is severed, the *ālayavijñāna* abandons the body and departs, following karma and the mind to take form within the six realms. It is like the two lines concerning a person’s debt.

This means that those whose karma is heavy receive retribution first. The two lines beginning with "The mind's threads are manifold" mean that those whose mental states are heavy fall into partiality.

The four lines beginning with "Impermanence" mean that time and life are driven by the rapid transition of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations); they do not abide for even a single thought-moment and cannot be extended or awaited.
The four lines beginning with "Human beings" mean that it is not only humans who are thus; this applies to all within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Within [this world], none can escape the cycle of transmigration, revolving like a turning wheel; how could it be measured by mere kalpas?
The "three existences" (tridhātu) refers to the three realms.

Moved by deep sorrow and struck with amazement, one laments with a heart pierced by grief: how could one remain silent? We must exhort one another, for what we regret is that we have been born together in this same world.
Since the age of the Sage has long passed and the Buddha-dharma has grown obscure, many people have become indolent; I briefly set forth my humble views to enlighten those who come after.
If one does not eliminate self-conceit, it will be difficult to escape the cycle of rebirth.
This summarizes the first four lines of the preceding text: witnessing the prevailing corruptions, one’s heart is moved by deep sorrow; how could one remain silent?

Thus, they exclaim together to admonish one another, uttering sounds of lamentation. "To seal one's speech" means to close one's mouth and remain silent. As for the final four lines beginning with "What is regrettable":
it means that the faculties of human beings have become indolent due to the influence of the times. "The Age of Images" refers to the Dharma-Ending Age (*kalpa*).

The Buddha’s True Dharma (*saddharma*) and Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) each lasted for a thousand years, while the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*) lasts ten thousand years. Now, we are at the end of the Semblance Dharma; thus it is called the "Age of Semblance.
This briefly explains the latter four lines, which clearly manifest the admonition. An ancient saying goes: "To look at a leopard through a tube, one sees only a single part.
This is a humble expression used to eliminate self-importance. "Self-conceit" (*jing*) refers to the strictness of one's observance. "Wheel" (*lun*).

"To turn one's back and flee" means that even after such earnest exhortation, if one does not eliminate old habits and abandon former attachments, how could one possibly evade the sufferings of birth and death?
How could one ever escape them by turning away?
The True Cause for Leaving Home According to the Three Clarities:

Now, one who leaves home sets out with a resolve that transcends the mundane; their mind and form differ from the laity as they perpetuate the lineage of the Sages and strike terror into the armies of Māra.
This is done to repay the four debts of gratitude and to deliver beings from the three realms of existence. If it were otherwise, one would merely be a pretender among the ranks of the Sangha.

"Setting out to transcend the mundane world" means that at the moment one sets out with a single thought to leave the household life, one’s resolve is to soar far beyond the dusty realm of the world and transcend the sphere of the profane.
"Mind and form differ from the secular" means that while the difference in form is evident, there are four ways in which the mind differs:

first, the desire to perpetuate the noble lineage of the sages so that the seeds of the Buddha are never severed but remain flourishing and prosperous; second, the desire to awe and subdue... [text truncated]
1. To cause the demonic armies to retreat and the false teachings to diminish; 2.

To repay the four debts of gratitude and bear their benevolent virtues—the four debts being those owed to one's parents, sentient beings, the king, and the Three Jewels; 3. To uproot the three realms of existence out of compassion for those submerged in suffering;
4. [To manifest] these four are the practices of attaining Buddhahood, subduing demons, repaying kindness, and saving the multitudes. These are the four.
Their conduct and dwelling differ from the common world, and thus they are far removed from it;

yet, if one possesses this physical form while lacking this mind, they are merely wearing my robes and mingling promiscuously among the ranks of the monastic community—how could such a person truly be a member of the Sangha Jewel?
My words and deeds have been negligent and coarse, yet I have vainly received offerings of faith. The places I frequented in years past remain unchanged by even a single step;

my life has passed in a blur—upon what can I rely? Moreover, these dignified monastic forms and observant countenances are all the result of roots of goodness planted in former lives, manifesting such extraordinary retribution.
Yet, if one intends merely to stand upright with hands folded, cherishing not even an inch of time, and fails to be diligent in one's practice, how can there be any fruit of merit?
If one cannot achieve success through no cause, how could one possibly spend a lifetime in vain? Furthermore, it would provide no benefit for future karma.
This clarifies the intent behind being improperly included among the ranks; by contrast, it shows that those who leave home with the correct cause are not like this.

The two phrases regarding "words and deeds" mean that when words and deeds contradict one another, one lacks the virtue required of a worthy recipient of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*) and merely consumes the food of others in vain. Regarding the phrase "in former years," [the following applies]:
The first phrase means that although one has left the household life, their worldly conduct remains unchanged and they have heard nothing of new virtue;

they are in a state of daze. The second phrase means that they have wasted their entire life in confusion, failing to cultivate merit or deeds, and having no good to rely upon—let alone the following ten phrases which serve as exhortations and encouragement, meaning that by experiencing beautiful retributions, one realizes and verifies past causes in the present.
What benefit will there be in practicing later?
Having bid farewell to my kin and resolved to don the black robes, I desire to transcend [suffering] equally; what need is there for morning or evening deliberations?

How could I delay until the time has passed? My heart’s aspiration is to become a pillar of the Buddha-dharma and serve as a mirror for those who come after. Constantly reflecting thus, yet I have not yet been able to...
This corresponds in part.
Examining the intent behind the first four lines—what indeed is the purpose of leaving the household life? Is it not to ascend above the various sages and transcend the common world below?
One must certainly contemplate this day and night and strive diligently to advance on the Path; how could one afford to delay?
"Passing the days and months in idle play"—the latter four lines refer to two things: being a pillar for the Buddha-dharma and serving as a mirror for future generations.
These two are indeed what the mind aspires to; yet, if one's power and effort are not sufficient, one cannot even correspond with them to a small degree.
How much less so if one is indolent, indulges the passions, and fails to exert oneself—how then can one repay the original vow of leaving the household life? "Pillar" refers to...
The Dharma-gate is the true material for a mirror of reflection;

it is called the master for those who study later. When one speaks, it must involve the classical texts; when one discourses, it should rely upon antiquity. One’s physical demeanor must be upright and resolute, and one’s temperament lofty and detached.
Essential conduct requires the assistance of virtuous friends, whom one must frequently bring before one's eyes and ears. As for one's dwelling, one must choose companions with care at all times.
Because one hears what was previously unheard at this time, it is said: "My parents gave me birth; my friends have perfected me.
The first four lines demonstrate the virtue of self-reliance: consulting the classics and examining antiquity means one must not indulge in theories born of mere personal fancy;
maintaining lofty intent and composed spirit means one must not approach the mannerisms of the vulgar. The final six lines clarify the principles for choosing friends.
The merit of this [practice] lies in the fact that during all intervals of walking and staying, one relies upon virtuous friends for guidance and the increase of one's learning;
thus, one must exercise skillful discernment. "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who complete me are my friends" is an ancient proverb.
This means that although parents can give birth to one’s physical body, it is through their earnest exhortation and their pointing out of flaws that they fashion and perfect one’s virtue and deeds.
Only a true spiritual friend can bring this about.

Associating with the virtuous is like walking through mist and dew; though it does not soak one's clothes, there is a constant, subtle moisture. Conversely, those who habituate themselves to evil cultivate their own ignorance and views;
they commit evil morning and night, receiving retribution even as they live, and after death, they sink into the depths. Once lost, they forfeit their humanity.
Even if one’s body were not to be reborn for ten thousand kalpas, how could one fail to engrave upon one’s heart that "honest words are逆耳" (contrary to the ear)?

This comparison of the benefits and harms of choosing friends means that by associating with the virtuous, although one may not consciously perceive their goodness, through the process of mutual intimacy and attachment, one’s evil thoughts are unconsciously and secretly dissolved, and one is silently imbued by the wind of their virtue. Thus it is said: [The original Chinese text continues here].
It is like walking through mist and dew: although they do not wet one's clothes, there is nevertheless a constant moisture.

Those who associate with and habituate themselves to evil, though they do not see its wickedness, will—in the midst of such intimacy and practice—unawares lose their innate goodness and secretly nurture their evil views;
hence it is said that "morning and evening they create evil. This refers to the immediate retribution manifest before one's eyes.

This refers to retribution after death, including both immediate retribution (*sahaja-vipāka*) and subsequent retribution (*paścāt-kāla-vipāka*). Once one loses this human body, it may not be regained for ten thousand kalpas;
as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Those who lose their human bodies are like the soil of the great earth, while those who obtain a human body are like the soil on a fingernail.
Having lost it, how difficult it is to think of regaining it! That which is contrary to the ear is, as the ancients said, a "good medicine."
"Harsh words benefit the illness; loyal speech is contrary to the ear but beneficial for practice. To "engrave it on the heart" means to inscribe it upon one's will so as not to forget.
The Master said of himself, "What I have spoken is indeed contrary to the ear, yet it is truly beneficial for practice.
Should students not engrave this in their hearts and strive to put it into practice?"
One is then able to wash the mind and nurture virtue, to obscure one's traces and conceal one's fame, and to store up the essence of the spirit while bringing all clamor and noise to a complete halt.
These words are an inscription on the power of the mind; they describe the efficacy of putting them into practice. Thus it says, "one is then able," and so forth.

"Washing the mind and nurturing virtue" means purifying the three poisons and cultivating the three trainings. "Obscuring traces and concealing fame" means hiding the illusory body and setting aside empty renown. "Storing up the essence of the spirit" [refers to...]

"Spirit" refers to the accumulation of the spiritual essence so that it does not manifest superficially; it is the merit of being naturally pure and free from defilement through the practice of cleansing and nurturing.
"The cessation of clamor" refers to the clamor of the mundane world; it is the merit of bringing the mundane world to a halt and remaining hidden and concealed.
Fourth, showing the path for entering the Way:

if one wishes to engage in Chan meditation and study the Way to transcend the gates of expedient means directly, all that has been clarified above concerns the matters of restraining body and mind and tempering one's will; now, the actual entry into the Way is shown.
Because there are sharp and dull faculties among those who follow the path via the roots [of practice], Chan and Teaching are divided into two types.

This indicates the aspiration and inclination of one who wishes to engage in Chan. "Chan" refers to the Supreme Vehicle Chan transmitted by Dharma, which is what is called "directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "suddenly transcending expedient means," this is because practicing and realizing according to the teachings generally belongs to...
The expedient means consist solely in the single matter of Chan meditation; through sudden awakening to one's own nature, one transcends all other expedients.
When the mind accords with the profound ford, one investigates the subtle essentials, discerns the deep mysteries, and awakens to the true source.

This clarifies the method of investigation through practice: setting aside all expedient means, one directly probes the fundamental nature until, suddenly, the mind accords with that nature—this is called "the mind’s accord with the profound source.

Although it is said that the mind accords with the nature, there is a fear that one may perceive only its coarse aspects and not its subtle essence, or perceive only its superficial breadth and not its essential core; such would be a mere superficiality.

How can one with shallow insight maintain a state of coarse indifference? One must investigate the subtle nuances, gathering the refined from the coarse and extracting the essential from the superficial.
Once the refined essence is attained, the realization of principle may indeed be called profound and mysterious;
yet though the principle is profound and mysterious, it remains merely an object perceived by the discriminating mind, and is not where the patch-robed monks of our tradition abide.
In one's practice, one must be precise in discernment, stripping away layer after layer; one must not settle into what is called the "profound and mysterious.

Furthermore, such a state must be criticized. When one has exhausted the profound to its ultimate limit—where there is no depth into which to enter and no mystery in which to dwell—and all achievement merges with the ordinary, only then can it be called the awakening to the true source; this is what is termed "the Real."
The "Source" refers to the source of the profound ford.
To inquire extensively from those who possess prior realization and to draw near to virtuous friends—this school’s subtle essence is difficult to attain; one must apply oneself with meticulous care.

This indicates the criteria for acceptance or rejection: that a student practicing Chan must not follow their own mind or take themselves as the authority while they have not yet attained realization.
One must rely on teachers and friends for definitive discernment; once this has been attained, one must further seek the testimony and verification of teachers and friends.

For this school does not fall within the scope of conceptual measurement, and its subtlety is difficult to grasp. It is said that "a difference of a hair's breadth results in worlds as far apart as heaven and earth";
therefore, one must be meticulous and must not treat it with negligence.
One may suddenly awaken therein to the True Cause, which is precisely the gradual stage for transcending the mundane world.

This involves shattering the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms and realizing that all internal and external phenomena are entirely unreal, arising from the transformations of the mind, and are all merely provisional names.

This clearly explains that the object of awakening can be realized within; what is here called the "correct cause within" refers to the original, inherent *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature) of the person.
The triple world is collectively termed the "twenty-five states of existence" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). A verse enumerating them separately states:
"The four continents, the four evil destinies, the six heavens of desire, and the Brahma heavens, the four dhyānas, the four formless realms, the realm of non-perception, and the five *anāgāmins*."

Regarding the refutation of external phenomena—namely the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), body, and mind—it means that when a practitioner of Chan attains awakening, it is like suddenly waking from a great dream;
the three realms and so forth are all merely objects within a dream, so how could they not be completely refuted?
The following passage explains the reason for this refutation: all phenomena are unreal and are entirely transformations of one's own mind.
They manifest and arise, yet they possess nothing more than provisional names.

When deluded, one does not know this and mistakes these names for reality, falsely giving rise to acceptance and rejection—like a small child playing with mirror-images or a thirsty deer chasing a mirage—is this not truly laughable?
Nanyue showed his disciples, saying: "All phenomena arise from the mind; the mind has no place of origin, and phenomena have no place of origin."
If one reaches the ground of the mind in one's dwelling, there will be no obstruction in what is done; yet this is not for those of superior faculties, so one must be cautious with words.
Alas! This can only be discussed with the wise.
Do not attempt to direct the mind toward a point of rest; simply let the emotions not attach to objects, and how could objects hinder the person? Let the *dharmatā* be all-pervasive as it may.
The flow is neither severed nor continued; hearing sounds and seeing forms are merely the ordinary. Whether "on this side" or "on that side," its application is never lacking.
This clarifies the merit of practice after awakening: the first three phrases dispel mundane conditions, while the latter two lines allow them to be as they are.
The two lines regarding "maintaining the dharma-nature" and "hearing sounds" integrate the practice with the ordinary state. The Fourth Patriarch showed this to Niutou, saying:
"When objective conditions have neither good nor bad, good and bad arise from the mind. If the mind does not apply arbitrary names, from where would deluded sentiments arise?
Since deluded sentiments do not arise, the true mind is left to its pervasive knowing. You need only follow the mind in its freedom, without further opposition."
"Governance" (treatise) is precisely named the eternally abiding Dharmakāya, which is without change; this may be understood by correlating it with the three preceding sections in order.

The final two phrases clarify that its application is never lacking: at this very moment, on the "other shore," it appears and disappears according to conditions and circumstances, without fixed rules.

If one’s conduct and stillness are such as this, one truly does not wear the Dharma robes in vain; it is also a way to repay the four debts of gratitude and deliver beings from the three realms of existence.
If one can remain non-retrogressive throughout successive lives, the stage of Buddhahood may certainly be expected.

As a guest traveling through the three realms, appearing and disappearing to serve as an example for others—this single study is most wondrous and profound. Provided you possess the heart of resolve, you will surely not be deceived.

This "binding benefit" refers to the intent of vigorous exhortation so that one does not regress; it means that the mirror of the mind is bright and pure, remaining unclouded even when passing through the barrier of death (*yinyin*).
"Buddha-stage" refers to the levels for attaining Buddhahood, namely the three stages of worthiness (*sānxián*) and the ten stages of sagehood (*shíshèng*).
"Not deceiving one another" is as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. Some say that the investigation of the ultimate is sudden.

One who has attained awakening is called a Buddha the very moment a single thought does not arise. Yet now you say that sudden awakening is the primary cause, which is merely the first step in gradually transcending the mundane world;
and you further say that if one can never retreat from this state of constant birth, the stage of Buddhahood can certainly be expected.
Is it not the case that even for one who has already awakened, there remains the danger of regression, and thus the necessity of gradual cultivation? The answer is: As the sutra says—

The statement that "the non-arising of a single thought is itself called Buddhahood" refers to the realization of principle; in terms of phenomena, this is not the case. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Though the principle is realized all at once, that which is realized is simultaneously extinguished; phenomena are not suddenly eliminated, for they are exhausted through gradual stages.
Furthermore, a monk asked Master Muzhou (Huishan): "For one who has attained sudden enlightenment, is there still further cultivation? The Master replied: [as follows].
If one truly awakens to the fundamental source, they know it for themselves; at that time, "cultivating" and "not cultivating" are merely dualistic expressions.

Now, when a beginner, following conditions, suddenly awakens to the principle of their own nature, although there still remain habitual tendencies from beginningless time that cannot be instantly purified, they are simply taught to cleanse the flowing consciousnesses of present karma—this is cultivation. One must not teach them as if there were some separate dharma.

Regarding the passage "He practices and inclines toward... and so forth, the single phrase "purifying the flowing consciousness of present karma" was something over which the ancients spent an incalculable amount of effort—like salt and sauce—by the waterside and beneath the trees; how could it be said that one realization is all that is required?

If there are those of middling capacity who are unable to transcend suddenly, they should nevertheless apply their minds to the teachings, diligently study the palm-leaf manuscripts, thoroughly investigate the principles and meanings, and propagate them through chanting and exposition to guide future generations.
In this way, they repay the Buddha’s kindness and ensure that their time is not spent in vain.
They must certainly use these practices to support themselves and maintain their dignified deportment; such individuals are true vessels of the Dharma within the Sangha.

This demonstrates the practice of the teachings, meaning that Chan meditation—which enters directly with a single blade and transcends all expedient means—is not something that those of middling or inferior capacity can achieve;
therefore, it is intended that they first apply their minds to the teachings so that, through hearing and understanding, they may gain faith and entry.

"Teachings" refers to the sūtras and śāstras written on *palm leaves* (*pattra*) in the Western Regions—materials used there for transcribing scriptures—just as paper and silk are used here in this land.

"Thoroughly investigating" refers to becoming proficient in the refined texts; "meticulously searching" refers to exhausting the meaning of the teachings. To chant, propagate, and disseminate these is what is meant by acting as a Great Dharma Master to widely spread the True Teaching.
To guide future generations and repay the Buddha’s kindness and virtue, the Sūtra says:

"Even if one were to carry [the scriptures] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as dust motes, or use one's body as a seat throughout the trichiliocosm, if one does not transmit the Dharma for the benefit [of others], [it is of no avail]."

Since sentient beings ultimately have no means by which to repay [the Buddha's kindness], one repays the Buddha’s grace only by practicing as taught for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others.
At that time, the four lines below refer to those of middling and inferior capacity who must rely on the support of the teachings;
yet even so, their time will not be spent in vain, as their four modes of conduct (*catur-īryāpatha*) will naturally accord with the proper measure.
This person is a vessel of the Dharma within the Sangha; a "vessel of the Dharma" refers to one who is a receptacle for receiving the Dharma.
Have you not seen how the climbing vine that clings to a pine tree soars to a height of a thousand fathoms? It is only by relying on such an excellent cause that it can bring about vast benefit.
This concludes the preceding two sections. The pine represents the religious teaching and the kudzu represents the student; one seeks the eight-foot [height] by means of them.
That is to say, the kudzu relies upon the tall pine to manifest its soaring potential of a thousand fathoms, and the monk relies upon the religious teaching to cultivate the benefit of vastness;
both arise from the excellence of their mutual support.

Diligently cultivate the fasts and precepts; do not let them be neglected or transgressed. From life to life and birth to birth, the extraordinary and wondrous causes and effects cannot be treated with casual indifference as you pass the days and spend your time in dull stagnation.
It is a pity that you waste this precious time without seeking spiritual advancement, merely squandering the offerings of the faithful from the ten directions and failing the four debts of gratitude.
As these accumulations deepen, the dust of the mind easily blocks the way, causing obstructions at every turn—a condition shared by all people.
Regarding self-contempt, it has been said of old: "Since he is a man of great capacity, so am I; one should not disparage oneself and yield in spirit.
If one does not act thus, then though remaining within the monastic gates, one will merely let a lifetime pass in vain, yielding no benefit whatsoever.

The above clearly elucidates the religious teachings, while this section concurrently demonstrates the precepts and laws; it means that one must not merely rely on the level of insight while casting aside ritual practice.
The first two lines mean that the observance of the fast and precepts must be cultivated with earnest sincerity and must not be deficient or transgressed.
The subsequent two lines mean that once the root of the precepts is complete, the superior rewards of humans and devas will never be lost. Not so.
One may casually disregard the intent of repeated exhortations; "stolidly ignorant" describes a state of mind.
As accumulation deepens, karma becomes increasingly heavy; as the dust of the mind easily obstructs, delusion grows ever deeper. The rest is self-evident.
I offer these five points of earnest exhortation and entreaty:
I hope you will rouse a resolute and fierce will and open a mind of exceptional penetration.
In all your actions, look to those of the highest caliber rather than following the vulgar and base. You must make this decision for yourself this very life; it cannot be left to others.
"Looking up and aspiring" means to have expectations; when one's will is resolute, there is no longer the habit of stubbornness, cowardice, or sycophancy.

"Maintaining a unique discernment" means to possess a capacity free from meanness, shallowness, narrowness, or confinement. The two phrases regarding conduct are from the *Analects*: "Upon seeing the virtuous, think of emulating them;
upon seeing those who are not virtuous, examine yourself within. The two lines regarding this present life are from an ancient saying: "If this body does not [strive] in this life..."
If one is born into the realm of transmigration, toward what further birth would one proceed? This body must also be transcended;

furthermore, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Ānanda said, "I thought that the Tathāgata would bestow upon me samādhi, but I did not know that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable. Therefore, one must resolve this for oneself.

When the mind is stilled and conditions cease, it no longer opposes the various sensory objects; the mind is empty and the environment is tranquil. This is simply because one has long been obstructed by stagnation.
One should read this text thoroughly and use it to admonish oneself from time to time.
Once the internal mind is stilled, external conditions will naturally vanish, and there will be no further duality. For the mind and its objects are fundamentally...
Emptiness and stillness are merely long obstructed by deluded sentiments, such that one cannot achieve sudden, thorough penetration;
the latter two lines admonish against forgetfulness, carrying the intent of a warning and an exhortation.
Do not forcibly assume a sense of mastery, nor follow the whims of human sentiment; being dragged along by the fruits of karma, it is truly difficult to escape—the resonance follows the sound.
When the form is straight, the shadow is upright; cause and effect are clearly manifest. How could one not feel anxiety and dread? Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Even if one were to pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, the karma one has created will not be forgotten. When the conditions and causes meet, the retribution must be received by oneself.
Thus we know that the punishments and entanglements of the triple world kill people. Exert yourselves in diligent cultivation; do not let the days pass in vain.

This is set forth in detail to explain the causes and effects, the transgressions and blessings, within the three realms, so that one may exercise self-restraint and caution rather than following worldly sentiments.

Regarding the fact that the karma one creates is never forgotten, the Sūtra says: "It is like writing characters in the dark; when the fire is extinguished, the characters remain. When the retribution of the fruit ripens, one receives it oneself.
This is illustrated by the World-Honored One receiving the retribution of eating horse-ears grain, and the Śākyas suffering the execution by Virūḍhaka—all of which were repayments for past deeds.
This is the remote cause.

Only when one deeply understands the faults and afflictions will one truly exhort others to practice and uphold [the teachings], vowing that for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of births, we shall everywhere be dharma companions.
The first two lines mean that because one has deeply understood the faults and afflictions, one is exhorted to practice and uphold [the Dharma], for it is not false or deceptive.

The latter two lines are a vow: if one can indeed believe these words and practice this conduct, then at all times and in all places, one will encounter others through the Dharma and become a Dharma-companion;
for those whose aims and ways coincide will naturally meet.
The second inscription is as follows: "This illusory body is like a dream-house; its forms and colors are but things in empty space.
In antiquity, basins, bowls, stools, and walking sticks all bore inscriptions to record words of admonition; now these words are appended at the end."
The intention behind these inscriptions is likewise so; furthermore, the restatement of the preceding meaning is like the *udāna* (spontaneous verses) found within the sūtras.

The "illusory body" (*māyā-deha*) is the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*). As the verse of Vipaśyin Buddha says: "The body receives birth from within the formless, just as various forms and appearances emerge from an illusion.
The "dream-house" refers to the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*), meaning that the triple world is unreal.

It is like a house within a dream or objects appearing in the sky; this reiterates the meaning of the "superior dream" regarding the primary and secondary [receptacle worlds], signifying that while they appear to exist, they are in reality non-existent.

Since the prior limit is infinite, how could the subsequent limit ever be reached? Emerging from here and sinking there, rising and falling, one cannot avoid the exhaustion of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).
When will there be rest?
The cycle of birth and death within the three realms is like a revolving wheel; seeking its beginning, it has no start, and tracing its end, it has no finish.
Sentient beings emerge and submerge, rise and sink, circling and returning within this sea of suffering until their forms and spirits are exhausted.
It is extreme; only by exiting the three realms can one perhaps escape it. Otherwise, one does not know when rest will come.
Clinging to the world, the subtle conditions form a substantial reality; from birth until old age, there is nothing at all gained.
Fundamental ignorance causes one to be deluded thereby.
The sentient beings of the world are merely the five aggregates (skandhas) conditioned by the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
That which is "non-apprehensible" refers to this body, which is but a provisional combination of aggregates and conditions and is fundamentally non-apprehensible;
it is only because sentient beings are deluded by fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā) that they falsely give rise to craving and attachment.
Time is precious; a single moment is unpredictable. This life passes in vain, and the next will be obstructed.
Regarding "time is precious," the ancients said: "A foot of jade is not as valuable as a wise person; an inch of time is what one should strive for. Thus, it is indeed precious.
Regarding "a single moment is unpredictable," the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* states: "Human life lies between a breath in and a breath out; how can it be taken for granted?"
The latter two phrases refer to the fact that if this present life has already been spent in vain, then future lives will become increasingly obstructed;
"obstructed" means that the mind and spirit grow ever more clouded and dull, becoming further impaired in their functioning.
Accumulating delusion upon delusion, all is due to the six thieves; one wanders back and forth through the six paths and crawls about within the three realms.
This corresponds to the first phrase of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*: "From various false thoughts, they successively cause one another;
accumulating delusion upon delusion, thus passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust. As for the latter three phrases of the sutra, it says: "Then your present eye..."
"The ears, nose, tongue, as well as body and mind—these six act as intermediaries for thieves who plunder the family's treasures.
Because of this, sentient beings have been bound by entanglements since beginningless time; thus, they are unable to transcend the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). The commentary states:

"The six realms are the primary retribution (*vipāka*), which is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*). The three realms are the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is the physical world."
"To go back and forth crawling" means to be entangled and unable to transcend;
"crawling" refers to prostrating on the ground and moving by hands, which is the mark of sentient beings' delusion and inversion.
Seek out enlightened masters early on and draw near to those of high virtue to resolve the nature of body and mind, thereby clearing away the thorns [of delusion].

The above passages serve as exhortations regarding the impermanence of birth and death and the confusion of inverted views; they demonstrate that for one who practices Chan, the teacher is a model for humanity.
Thus, when the ancients had not yet clarified their own fundamental matter, they did not shrink from diligent toil, traversing mountains and rivers.
Seeking out masters and visiting friends to discern the heterodox from the authentic, dispel delusions, and clarify the Way, he ultimately refused to sit idly by or remain mired in ignorance.
With his own mind thus resolved, like Xuefeng, Yantou, and Qinshan, he formed friendships and traveled to study under various teachers;
he visited Touzi three times and went to Dongshan nine times. That they all later became great vessels was not due to the power of their teachers and friends? Therefore, he went to seek instruction.
A practitioner of dhyāna must seek out a wise teacher of high virtue early on and draw near to them; in this way,
they may have their doubts regarding the true and the false resolved, and restrain their body and mind to cut away the thorns—
these thorns and poisonous spines being the non-virtues of body and mind, as well as all manner of improper defects.
The world is inherently floating and empty; how could manifold conditions coerce it?
This is taught so that practitioners of dhyāna, who may fail to realize that worldly conditions are floating, empty, and illusory, do not encounter such coercion and thereby lose right mindfulness.
The Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang said: "All dharmas fundamentally do not themselves declare that they are empty."
He himself says that form is neither right nor wrong, neither defiled nor pure, and that there is no mind that binds people;

it is only that people themselves falsely conceptualize and construct various kinds of interpretations, give rise to various kinds of knowledge and views, and produce various kinds of attachments and fears.
One should simply understand that all phenomena do not arise of themselves, but all stem from one's own single thought of deluded imagination.
By grasping signs erroneously, one fails to realize that the mind and its objects fundamentally do not reach one another;
rather, there is liberation in their respective places, each and every phenomenon is quiescent in its own place, and each is a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in its own place.
Investigate the principles of the Dharma, taking awakening as the standard.
"Investigation" refers to the practice of critical inquiry; "principles of the Dharma" refers to one's fundamental duty. To "take awakening as the standard" means to take awakening as the model.
For the Great Way is vast and remote, possessing no fixed path; when students seek it through inquiry, they should simply act thus.
To take awakening as one's standard, one must not fail to attain it. What is called "awakening" is like suddenly remembering after having forgotten, or like suddenly waking from a dream;
it is like meeting one’s own biological parents at a crossroads—what further doubt could there be?
How could this be compared to a knowledge based on mere analogies or a vision born of a hazy state, while falsely claiming to have attained awakening? Long ago, Dahui Zonggao...
The Chan Master was naturally gifted and possessed a sharp tongue; all quarters of the Buddhist world certified his realization.
Yet Xuedou Gao alone knew he had not yet attained awakening, so he shook his head and departed, saying, "How could a man of great character willingly swallow such wild fox drool?
Finally, he went to Tianning to study under Yuanwu, whereupon he said to himself, "If this old fellow..."
Because he had composed the *Wu chan lun* (Treatise on the Absence of Meditation), Yuanwu went to see him to test his realization. Yuanwu showed him the essential tools of his own school’s forge;
Xuedou was thus humbled and submitted to his teaching. Subsequently, under Yuanwu’s guidance, Xuedou clarified the Great Dharma, penetrating it to its very core.
Possessing great capacity and great function, he became the foremost master of the Song dynasty—how could he be compared to those people of today who act in such a chaotic manner?
To accept [offerings] while harboring delusions and receiving the seal of approval from others is to deceive both teacher and disciple, bringing ruin upon oneself and misleading others;
thus, Mahāmati may serve as a mirror for all practitioners of Chan throughout the ages.
"Abandon both mind and objects; do not record, do not recall. Let the six sense-faculties be at ease, and let conduct and dwelling be silent and still.
This clarifies the state of initial awakening: although one knows that mind and objects are fundamentally empty, the shadows of mind and objects have not yet vanished.
One must apply the effort of abandonment; by neither recording nor recalling, the six sense-faculties and the four modes of deportment will naturally become so.
When one is settled in tranquility, one can achieve the Samādhi of One Mark and One Practice.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are simultaneously stilled;
because the mind arises, the myriad dharmas arise together. If the single mind does not arise, then the mind and its objects need not be discarded.
Since all things are themselves empty, what dharma could there be that would not cease? Master Suishi said, "The final phrase is where one finally reaches the secure barrier.
This concludes the *Miaoguo Weishan Jingce* (The Admonition of Master Weishan).
